name: LSQUIC (LiteSpeed QUIC)
workload: HTTP/3 download of an 8 GB file over a 10 Gbit/s link between two dedicated bare-metal hosts, using an extended QUIC Interop Runner. All client/server pairs of 6 QUIC libraries were measured with Cubic/Reno congestion control. The paper states 50 repetitions per pair for Fig. 3. The Fig. 10 rerun used 20 repetitions per pair (configs/configs/baseline-optimized.yml).
claimed_speedup: Fig. 3 (default builds, 8 GB HTTP/3 download, 10G link): LSQUIC-LSQUIC pair 3004 Mbit/s vs quiche-quiche pair 2506 Mbit/s (~1.2x, derived from page data). Fig. 10 (UDP receive buffer raised 32x to 6815744 B, both libraries rebuilt for the host CPU): LSQUIC*-LSQUIC* 3882 Mbit/s vs quiche*-quiche* 2590 Mbit/s (~1.5x, derived from page data). The heatmap values are per-pair means (checked against the artifact's processed.csv). The mixed pair of an LSQUIC server and a quiche client drops to 1186 Mbit/s (1616 in Fig. 10).
compiler_and_flags: From the artifact repo tumi8/quic-10g-paper. Fig. 3: LSQUIC commit f3657f1f is built by implementations/lsquic/build_default.sh with `cmake -DBORINGSSL_DIR=../boringssl .` and no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so lsquic's CMakeLists.txt defaults to Debug (-O0 -g3). BoringSSL a9670a8b uses a plain `cmake .`. quiche commit 95af1427 is built with `cargo build --release`. Fig. 10: LSQUIC* uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (-O3 -g0) plus patches/march.patch (-march=native, -DLSQUIC_LOWEST_LOG_LEVEL=LSQ_LOG_INFO). quiche* uses RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native' cargo build --release. The C compiler is GCC from Debian build-essential and Rust is the unpinned 'stable' rustup toolchain. No versions are recorded.
hardware: Default: AMD EPYC 7543 (32-core), Broadcom BCM57416 NIC, Debian Bullseye, kernel 5.10.0-8-amd64. Also repeated on AMD EPYC 7551P, Intel Xeon D-1518, Intel Xeon E5-1650, Intel Xeon Gold 6312U (paper Table I).
tradeoffs: Goodput is highly asymmetric by client/server combination: in this same study the quiche-server/LSQUIC-client pair reaches more than 2x the goodput of the LSQUIC-server/quiche-client pair, so the 'LSQUIC beats quiche' result holds for matched same-vendor pairs, not universally across mixed pairs. LSQUIC showed unintended retransmission behavior with BBR congestion control in this study (paper forced Cubic/Reno for all libraries to keep the comparison fair).
caveats: Peer-reviewed at IFIP Networking 2023 (Barcelona; DOI 10.23919/IFIPNetworking57963.2023.10186365, ISBN 978-3-903176-57-7). The code, configs and raw results are public (github.com/tumi8/quic-10g-paper), but the compiler versions are not stated, so the record is capped at B. The artifact build scripts show that the Fig. 3 LSQUIC binary was a default-Debug (-O0) build competing against release-built quiche, so that comparison understates LSQUIC. The paper's 'compile flags to optimize for the architecture' step (LSQUIC*) is really Debug to Release -O3 plus -march=native. The win holds only for LSQUIC on both ends: an LSQUIC server with a quiche client reaches just 1186 Mbit/s. The same group's 2026 NOMS follow-up (LSQUIC v4.2.0, quiche 0.23.2, Xeon Gold 6421N) shows a smaller lead of 3605 vs 3241 Mbit/s (~1.11x, derived), with MsQuic at 8250 Mbit/s well ahead of both.
found_via: arXiv API search_query=all:QUIC AND all:implementation AND all:performance -> arxiv.org/abs/2309.16395 'QUIC on the Highway: Evaluating Performance on High-rate Links'

Its Fig. 3 and Fig. 10 heatmaps show LSQUIC-LSQUIC 3004/3882 vs quiche-quiche 2506/2590 Mbit/s, and the values match the means in the artifact's results/baseline/client-timestamps/goracle*/processed.csv. The artifact repo tumi8/quic-10g-paper (configs/configs/baseline.yml, implementations/{lsquic,quiche}/build_*.sh, quic-interop-runner/) and the AMD EPYC 7543 CPU are public, and the flags can be derived from the build scripts. The metadata is verified: MIT, 1876 stars, last commit 2026-09-20, not archived.

name: LSQUIC-DPDK (tumi8 kernel-bypass fork)
workload: HTTP/3 download of an 8 GiB file between two bare-metal hosts with 100 Gbit/s Intel E810 NICs, using the extended QUIC Interop Runner (framework/config/bypass-paper/01-implementation-matrix.conf and 06-dpdk-integration.conf). Same-implementation client/server pairs ran 50 repetitions each. Kernel variants used 32x (6815744 B) socket buffers with NIC offloads on. DPDK variants ran on the physical function (ice) or an SR-IOV virtual function (iavf).
claimed_speedup: Paper Fig. 2 (plain DPDK, same-implementation pairs, mean of 50 x 8 GiB downloads): LSQUIC-DPDK 10756 Mbit/s vs upstream MsQuic v2.4.8 (kernel UDP with GSO+GRO) 8250 Mbit/s (~1.30x, derived from page data). MsQuic-DPDK reaches 7983 Mbit/s (~1.35x, derived), and upstream LSQUIC reaches 3605 Mbit/s (2.98x, printed). With SR-IOV (quic-bypass-paper measurement-data/06-dpdk-integration/processed.csv, Fig. 5): LSQUIC-DPDK 11019 vs MsQuic-DPDK 8118 (~1.36x) and quiche-DPDK 6168 Mbit/s (~1.79x) (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: LSQUIC-DPDK: quic-dpdk-implementations/lsquic-dpdk/build.sh builds BoringSSL 0.20250212.0 and lsquic-dpdk with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (-O3 -g0 via lsquic CMakeLists). It builds DPDK commit 1b3bf112 with meson -Dplatform=generic, using GCC from Debian 12 build-essential (version not stated). MsQuic-DPDK: build.ps1 -Static -Tls openssl -Config Release -UseDpdk with CFLAGS/CXXFLAGS=-Wno-error=stringop-overflow. The kernel baselines (MsQuic v2.4.8, LSQUIC, quiche) are built by a private LRZ GitLab CI, so their flags are unpublished.
hardware: Both hosts: Intel Xeon Gold 6421N (32 cores), 512 GiB DDR5, Intel E810-CQDA2 100 Gbit/s NIC, Debian 12 with Linux 6.1.0-17, DPDK v24.11 (paper Appendix Table I).
stars_or_usage: 0 stars (research artifact accompanying a NOMS 2026 paper)
tradeoffs: Same DPDK/SR-IOV deployment complexity as other entries in this family (dedicated NIC/queue, hugepages, root). A separate table in the same dataset (measurement-data/01-implementation-matrix/processed.csv) shows msquic-dpdk NOT beating vanilla kernel msquic (7982 vs 8250 Mbit/s), so DPDK's benefit is very implementation-dependent; only the head-to-head DPDK-vs-DPDK cross-library comparison used here is a clean win for LSQUIC-DPDK.
caveats: Peer-reviewed and published: Spaeth et al., 'Kernel Bypass Surgery: A Viable Procedure for Maximizing QUIC Bandwidth?', NOMS 2026, Rome, pp. 1-8, DOI 10.1109/NOMS69089.2026.11668379. The open preprint is on net.in.tum.de, and the dataset is Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.18630971. The two msquic-dpdk tables are not inconsistent: 7983 is plain DPDK on the ice PF and 8118 is SR-IOV on the iavf VF, which the paper finds slightly faster. The comparison pits kernel bypass against kernel sockets. LSQUIC-DPDK needs a DPDK-bound NIC port or SR-IOV VF, runs single-threaded with busy polling, and has no GSO/GRO. The authors note that their MsQuic-DPDK datapath enqueues packets one at a time, which handicaps it. Against upstream MsQuic with GSO+GRO, the lead is ~1.30x. GitHub does not mark the repo as a fork, but it is the full LSQUIC tree (based on v4.2.0) with a DPDK datapath.
found_via: Same discovery path as quiche-DPDK entry: gh api orgs/tumi8/repos -> tumi8/quic-bypass-paper -> measurement-data/06-dpdk-integration/processed.csv

verification.tier_reason: Peer-reviewed NOMS 2026 paper (now published, DOI 10.1109/NOMS69089.2026.11668379). Its Fig. 2 prints LSQUIC-DPDK 10756 vs upstream MsQuic 8250 and MsQuic-DPDK 7983 Mbit/s. The published processed.csv gives the claimed SR-IOV means (11019 / 8118 / 6168). The framework, configs, LSQUIC-DPDK build script (Release) and CPU (Xeon Gold 6421N) are public. It is not A: the compiler version is not stated, and the kernel MsQuic/LSQUIC/quiche baseline binaries are built from a private LRZ GitLab CI (framework/fetch_artifacts.py), so their flags are not published.

name: Nail (NailDNS demo server)
workload: Authoritative-DNS load test. 50,000 random dictionary-based domains (com/net/org), ~90% of them written to the zone file, so ~10% of queries get NXDOMAIN. Each domain is queried 0-3 times (per the paper) in shuffled order with BIND's queryperf, at most 20 outstanding queries, for 60 s. 7 runs with a daemon restart between runs, against ISC BIND 9.9.5 on the same local machine, one core.
claimed_speedup: median throughput ~139,215 qps (NailDNS) vs ~47,234 qps (BIND 9.9.5 per the paper text; the figure caption says 9.5.5), ~2.9x faster (derived from page data); median round-trip time 0.139 ms vs 0.416 ms (derived from page data, box plot of 7 runs each)
compiler_and_flags: NailDNS C server built with -std=gnu99 -O3 (examples/dns/Makefile); compiler not named (make default CC); BIND 9.9.5 build flags not stated
hardware: Intel i7-3610QM, single core, 12GB RAM (OSDI'14 paper, Performance subsection)
tradeoffs: NailDNS is a 295-line research demo built to showcase the Nail parser-combinator toolkit (grammar-driven parsing/generation with dependent fields and stream transforms); it implements only zone parsing, query answering, and label compression, none of BIND's dynamic reconfiguration, TSIG, notify, or DNSSEC-signing machinery. Not a drop-in BIND replacement.
caveats: Peer-reviewed OSDI'14 paper (USENIX, MIT CSAIL authors). The paper states the CPU (i7-3610QM, one core) and the repo ships the benchmark scripts, queryperf and raw results (examples/dns/bench), but the C compiler and BIND's build are unstated, so the tier is B, not A. The paper body says BIND 9.9.5 (2014), but the figure caption says 9.5.5, probably a caption typo. NailDNS is a minimal 183-line demo server that lacks many BIND features, and the test ran over loopback on one machine. Last commit was 2015 (abandoned).
found_via: GitHub code search: 'times faster than BIND' -> jbangert/nail paper/login/eval.tex and paper/osdi14/performance.tex

name: ngtcp2
workload: quicperf: an apples-to-apples C++ benchmark harness running the same shared TLS material, saturation policy, and socket backend (syscall/io_uring) against native adapters for ngtcp2, LSQUIC, TQUIC, quiche, picoquic, XQUIC and several Rust/Zig stacks, over loopback UDP with CUBIC congestion control. Scenarios include bulk download/upload, bidirectional transfer, multistream transfer, loss recovery, and flow-control-limited transfer.
claimed_speedup: ~1.5-2.1x quiche on bulk-transfer scenarios (p50, syscall backend, derived from page data): download 18.227 vs 11.258 Gbps (1.62x), upload 31.047 vs 14.794 Gbps (2.10x), bidirectional 20.503 vs 12.662 Gbps (1.62x), multistream download 16.459 vs 10.990 Gbps (1.50x), multistream upload 24.816 vs 15.291 Gbps (1.62x), loss-recovery 17.379 vs 11.689 Gbps (1.49x), flow-control 15.600 vs 10.309 Gbps (1.51x); io_uring backend 1.35-1.71x. In the same run ngtcp2 is slower than quiche on request/response (0.80x), stream churn (0.70x), small-payload messages (0.71x), 0-RTT request/response (0.70x), close/reset cleanup (0.70x), connect (0.41x), resumed connect (0.37x) and DATAGRAM rate (0.29x), all syscall.
compiler_and_flags: quicperf C++ harness: CMake Release, -O3, native CPU flags, LTO by default (per README). ngtcp2 1.22.1 built from the release tarball via depofiles/ngtcp2.DepoFile (CMake, static, BoringSSL main-beddb58 backend); that depofile sets no extra optimisation flags of its own. quiche 0.29.0 (cloudflare/quiche commit e85fc8e) built via depofiles/quiche.DepoFile with RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3", CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_LTO=fat, CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_CODEGEN_UNITS=1, --features ffi.
tradeoffs: C library requiring an external TLS backend (OpenSSL/BoringSSL/GnuTLS/wolfSSL/picotls) and manual event-loop integration, unlike quiche's more batteries-included Rust API. In the same quicperf harness ngtcp2 is markedly slower than quiche and most peers on connection-establishment rate (113 vs 277 conn/s, syscall) and on plain request/response rate (51,386 vs 64,574 rps), so its measured advantage is specific to sustained bulk-transfer throughput, not connection setup or small-request rate.
caveats: quicperf (victorstewart/quicperf, 27 stars) is an independent but small personal harness. Its committed run-environment file (docs/results/fixed-full-matrix-max16-20260601T175816Z/fixed-environment.txt) and adaptive-samples.tsv record only an anonymized machine_hash, with no CPU model, so hardware is not stated. That rules out Tier A, and the harness is not well known enough for B. The benchmark is loopback-only, with no physical or WAN link. The 2026-06-01 run was taken from a dirty working tree: the environment file's git status shows uncommitted edits to perf.ngtcp2.h, perf.quiche.h, perf.cpp and other adapters on top of commit 3eda036, so the committed code may not reproduce it exactly. The syscall download row (both libraries) and quiche's syscall bidirectional row are flagged 'inconclusive'. The publishable-only pairwise-comparisons.tsv still shows ngtcp2 winning upload, multistream, loss-recovery and flow-control rows at 1.35-2.10x. The win is limited to bulk transfer: ngtcp2 loses to quiche on every connection-setup and small-request scenario in the same run.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "ngtcp2" "benchmark" -> victorstewart/quicperf; numbers read directly from docs/latest-results.md and docs/methodology.md

name: picoquic
workload: quicperf loopback harness: Linux, C++-owned UDP I/O shared by all stacks, CUBIC, shared TLS 1.3 Ed25519 material, one pinned server thread. Upload is client-to-server bulk transfer (8-byte request plus bulk body, duration mode) on the syscall backend. picoquic ran with 2 client threads and quiche with 4; a saturation scout chose each library's thread count. Each row has 20 samples in 5 randomized blocks, and both rows are publishable. Also Connect (full handshake plus bidi stream creation, at most 128 handshakes per sample), syscall, 16 client threads each.
claimed_speedup: ~1.06-1.07x quiche on bulk upload and connection setup (p50, derived from page data): upload syscall 15.823 vs 14.794 Gbps (1.07x; pairwise 95% CI 1.061-1.076), upload io_uring 14.549 vs 13.755 Gbps (1.06x), connect syscall 297 vs 277 conn/s (1.07x; CI 1.049-1.095). In the same run picoquic is slower than quiche in the other 18 of 21 publishable pairwise comparisons, all syscall: request/response 59,098 vs 64,574 rps (0.92x), flow control 0.94x, loss recovery 7.590 vs 11.689 Gbps (0.65x), small-payload messages 0.67x, close/reset 0.66x, 0-RTT 0.86x, multistream download 0.546 vs 10.990 Gbps (0.05x) and multistream upload 0.591 vs 15.291 Gbps (0.04x). Its bidirectional (0.22 vs 12.66 Gbps) and DATAGRAM rows are inconclusive.
compiler_and_flags: quicperf C++ harness: CMake Release, C++20, -O3 -march=native, LTO (CMakeLists.txt, README); exact compiler/version not published. picoquic pinned at master commit 2b1e14d (2026-05-16) with picotls 7c32032 (fusion on) and OpenSSL 4.0.0 via depofiles/picoquic.DepoFile. quiche 0.29.0 (e85fc8e) built with RUSTFLAGS='-C target-cpu=native -C opt-level=3', fat LTO, codegen-units=1.
tradeoffs: picoquic is a minimal, largely single-threaded reference/research QUIC stack. It only leads quiche on 2 of 16 quicperf scenarios (Upload throughput, Connect rate); quiche wins the other 14, often by a wide margin (e.g. request/response 64,574 vs 59,098 qps, stream churn 74,756 vs 48,480 streams/s), so this is workload-specific, not general superiority.
caveats: quicperf (victorstewart/quicperf, 27 stars) is a small personal harness, not a well-known suite. Its author has 57 commits in private-octopus/picoquic, so the harness is not fully independent for this pair. docs/results/fixed-full-matrix-max16-20260601T175816Z/fixed-environment.txt records only an anonymized machine_hash (no CPU model). The 2026-06-01 run came from a dirty working tree, with uncommitted edits to perf.picoquic.h, perf.quiche.h and other adapters on commit 3eda036. Loopback only. The wins are narrow: ~6-7% on upload (both backends) and on syscall connect, and connect rates for all 12 stacks cluster at 234-306 conn/s. picoquic loses to quiche in 18 of 21 publishable pairwise comparisons, by 16-26x on multistream transfers.

name: quiche-DPDK (tumi8 kernel-bypass fork)
language: C (DPDK kernel-bypass I/O layer added on top of upstream Rust quiche core)

claimed_speedup: Paper Fig. 2 (same-implementation pairs, mean of 50 x 8 GiB HTTP/3 downloads): the quiche-DPDK client+server pair reaches 5937 Mbit/s vs 3241 Mbit/s for upstream quiche (kernel UDP, GSO on, 32x socket buffers), 1.83x as printed in the paper. With SR-IOV (measurement-data/06-dpdk-integration/processed.csv, Fig. 5), quiche-DPDK reaches 6168 Mbit/s (~1.90x vs 3241, derived from page data).

It builds the C DPDK client/server with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo and DPDK commit 1b3bf112 with meson -Dplatform=generic. The C compiler version is not stated. The kernel quiche baseline is built by a private LRZ GitLab CI, and its flags are unpublished.

stars_or_usage: 0 stars (research artifact accompanying a NOMS 2026 paper)
tradeoffs: DPDK requires dedicating a whole NIC/queue to userspace polling (no shared use with the kernel network stack), hugepages, and root/elevated privileges; adds substantial deployment complexity vs a drop-in library. The paper states that no quiche library code changed. The comparison pits kernel bypass (a DPDK-bound NIC port or SR-IOV VF, one polling thread) against kernel UDP sockets. quiche-DPDK is the slowest of the four DPDK stacks (LSQUIC-DPDK reaches 10756 Mbit/s) and is below upstream MsQuic with GSO+GRO (8250 Mbit/s). name: TQUIC
workload: quicperf: same shared C++ harness as the ngtcp2 entry, loopback UDP, CUBIC, shared TLS 1.3 Ed25519 material, one pinned server thread. A saturation scout chose the thread count; the published p50s come from 20 fixed randomized-block samples per row, with scout samples excluded.
claimed_speedup: ~2.4x quiche on request/message-rate scenarios (p50, syscall backend, derived from page data): request/response 155,043 vs 64,574 rps (2.40x), stream churn 178,272 vs 74,756 streams/s (2.38x), small-payload messages 176,604 vs 73,852 msgs/s (2.39x), 0-RTT request/response 154,448 vs 65,327 rps (2.36x), close/reset cleanup 178,364 vs 75,080 streams/s (2.38x); io_uring backend 3.0-3.4x. In the same run TQUIC is slower than quiche on every bulk-throughput row (download 8.600 vs 11.258 Gbps; 0.76-0.96x across download, upload, bidirectional, multistream, loss-recovery and flow-control, syscall), on resumed connect (216 vs 301 conn/s, 0.72x) and on DATAGRAM rate (0.17x).

name: picoquic-DPDK (Tyunyayev kernel-bypass fork)
workload: One QUIC connection downloading 20 GB (a picoTLS TCP+TLS reference ran a 30 s download) between a client and a server over a 100 Gbps link. claimed_speedup: Primary paper: "Compared to the original picoquic implementation, we see a 3x improvement" in single-connection goodput (abstract: "improving the throughput by a 3x factor"). For handshakes with 0-byte requests, picoquic-dpdk handles up to 6000 requests/s while picoquic manages about half that. The paper also says picoquic-dpdk on 1 core beats quiche, quicly and msquic; msquic reaches 10.6 Gbps with a 3-core pipeline.
hardware: Two Intel Xeon Silver 4314 CPUs @ 2.4 GHz (client and server) on a 100 Gbps link; the NIC model is not stated in the paper.
tradeoffs: DPDK kernel bypass requires a dedicated NIC/queue, hugepages, and root; README describes the project as 'work in progress'. A companion experiments repo (UCLouvain-ENSG/picoquic-dpdk-experiments) is explicitly set up to compare it against quicly, quiche, and msquic directly, but the specific numeric results for those comparisons could not be retrieved this session.

The paper names https://github.com/UCLouvain-ENSG/picoquic-dpdk as the official code (MIT, 3 stars, last commit 2022-10-31), with scripts in UCLouvain-ENSG/picoquic-dpdk-experiments (NPF, no license). name: libev
workload: Socket-pair event loop benchmark (libev's bench.c): active clients exchanging data plus idle timers, scaled from 100 to 100,000 file descriptors with 100 and 1,000 active clients, measuring per-iteration dispatch time and timeout-handling overhead.
claimed_speedup: libev 3.31 vs libevent 1.4.3 (both on epoll) using libevent's bench.c. With no timeouts, libevent takes 'almost twice as much time than libev' in total time per iteration (the gap grows with fd count), but the event-processing (poll) times differ by less than 5%. With per-connection idle timeouts, libev's event processing is 'consistently faster (with a factor of two to almost three)' over 100-100,000 fds, and overall time 'has been almost halved'. The 2011 appendix rerun (libev 4.03 vs libevent 1.4.13 and 2.0.10) shows the same pattern. All figures are from the page's prose; the charts carry no numeric tables.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 4.2.3, -O3 -fno-guess-branch-probability -g
hardware: Core2 Quad @ 3.6GHz, Debian GNU/Linux, kernel 2.6.24-1
stars_or_usage: 1,790 stars on the unofficial GitHub mirror (enki/libev). Node.js bundled it through v0.4 (deps/libev). The upstream page lists GNU Virtual Private Ethernet, rxvt-unicode, auditd and the Deliantra server and client as users.
tradeoffs: More manual/lower-level API than libevent or libuv (explicit watcher structs, no built-in cross-platform abstraction beyond POSIX backends); weaker Windows support; author himself notes libevent 2.x (much newer than the 1.4.3 tested here) narrowed some gaps.
caveats: enki/libev is an unofficial GitHub mirror stuck at libev 4.22 (Dec 2015). Upstream lives in schmorpforge CVS (http://software.schmorp.de/pkg/libev.html), and its latest release, 4.33, is from 2020-03-18. The benchmark is the libev author's own: the original run (libevent 1.4.3 vs libev 3.31) is from ~2008 and the writeup was last revised 2011-01-11 (version 6). The CPU is given only as 'Core2 Quad at 3.6GHz', and results are line charts, not tables. Without timeouts, the gain is almost entirely in watcher setup; poll times are within 5%. libuv is not covered. The independent bartman/event-loop-benchmark (5 stars, -Os -ggdb, no hardware stated) reuses this bench.c. In its README, libev's total is ~27.5k µs vs libevent's ~123k µs, but libevent's event-processing column is lower (~215 vs ~270 µs).

name: mTCP
workload: Short-lived TCP connection handling / small-message request-response transactions on multicore Linux, plus ported applications (e.g. lighttpd) comparing the user-level mTCP stack to the stock Linux TCP stack.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: small-message transactions 25x faster than the latest Linux TCP stack and 3x faster than MegaPipe (best prior research system); popular applications 33% to 320% faster than on Linux. Sec 5.1: at 8 cores the 64B-message benchmark is 25x vs Linux 3.10.12 without SO_REUSEPORT, 5x vs Linux with SO_REUSEPORT, and 3x vs MegaPipe; connection accept is 13x/7.5x/5x vs Linux/REUSEPORT/multiprocess. lighttpd (SpecWeb2009 static files) is 3.2x/2.2x/1.5x vs Linux/REUSEPORT/MegaPipe; the SSLShader proxy is +18% to +33%.
hardware: Server: 1x 8-core Intel Xeon E5-2690 @ 2.90 GHz, 32 GB RAM, Intel 82599 10 GbE NIC; mTCP on Linux 2.6.32 (PSIO), baseline Linux 3.10.12 (ixgbe-3.17.3), MegaPipe on Linux 3.1.3
tradeoffs: Requires a dedicated packet-I/O driver (DPDK, PacketShader, or netmap) and cores reserved for the mTCP stack; exposes its own epoll-like API rather than drop-in POSIX sockets, so applications must be ported.
caveats: NSDI 2014 peer-reviewed paper; the CPU is stated but the compiler and flags are not, so the tier is B. The headline 25x is against Linux WITHOUT SO_REUSEPORT (a shared accept queue); against Linux with SO_REUSEPORT the gain is 5x at 8 cores. The baseline apps use the kernel's BSD sockets + epoll (the paper's Fig. 2 shows accept()/epoll_wait() vs mtcp_accept()/mtcp_epoll_wait()). The 2014 results used the PSIO driver on Linux 2.6.32. The core is BSD-3-Clause (GitHub reports NOASSERTION because of the template '<organization>' placeholder), but io_engine/ (PSIO driver) is GPL-2.0 and the dpdk submodule has its own licenses. There have been no commits on master since 2019-11.

claimed_speedup: Abstract: 2-5x lower latency and 9x higher throughput for Redis relative to a well-tuned Linux implementation (2x read latency, 5x write latency, 9x write throughput). hardware: CPU not stated; Linux 5.10 kernel

name: F-Stack
workload: Nginx serving a fixed body. CPS (Connection: close, 600-byte body), RPS (keep-alive, 600-byte body) and bandwidth (keep-alive, 3.7 KB body) on 1-24 physical cores. Kernel Nginx (Linux default config with all softirqs on core 0; 'si' = per-IRQ smp_affinity spread; 'Reuseport' = reuseport in nginx.conf) vs Nginx+F-Stack (DPDK kernel bypass plus a ported FreeBSD TCP/IP stack; body returned directly from nginx.conf). Intel XL710 40GbE NIC.
claimed_speedup: README 'Nginx Testing Result' charts. Bandwidth values are the printed data labels; RPS/CPS values are approximate, read off the right axis of the chart images. CPS (Connection: close, 600-byte body, 1-20 cores): Nginx+F-Stack 5.82 Gbit/s (~1.04M CPS) vs Nginx 'si' (kernel, IRQ smp_affinity spread, no reuseport) 0.47 Gbit/s (~86k CPS) at 20 cores, ~12x (derived from page data). CPS_Reuseport (Connection: close, different test environment, 1-16 cores): F-Stack 5.78 Gbit/s (~1.02M CPS) vs Nginx+reuseport 2.47 (~0.44M) vs default Nginx 0.63 (~0.11M) at 16 cores, ~2.3x vs reuseport (derived from page data). RPS (keep-alive, 600-byte body, 1-24 cores): F-Stack 26.96 Gbit/s (~4.77M RPS) vs Nginx si 18.49 (~3.27M) vs default Nginx 2.11 (~0.38M) at 24 cores, ~1.46x vs the tuned kernel and ~12.8x vs the default config (derived from page data). Bandwidth (keep-alive, 3.7 KB body, 1-16 cores): F-Stack leads at low core counts (4.30 vs 2.90 Gbit/s at 1 core, 33.75 vs 23.28 at 8 cores, ~1.45x derived from page data), but both hit the ~37.1 Gbit/s 40GbE ceiling at 16 cores (parity). The README headline '10 million concurrent connections, 5 million RPS, 1 million CPS' under full NIC load: the 5M RPS and 1M CPS figures roughly match the charts, while the 10M-connection figure has no supporting chart.
hardware: Intel XL710 40GbE QSFP+ NIC, Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3 @ 2.30GHz (NUMA), 128GB RAM, CentOS 7.2, kernel 3.10.104-1-tlinux2 (the CPS_Reuseport chart was run in a different, unstated environment)
license: BSD-2-Clause for F-Stack's main code, per the LICENSE file (GitHub reports 'Other'/NOASSERTION). Bundled components: DPDK BSD-3-Clause (kernel modules GPL-2.0), FreeBSD stack BSD-4-Clause, Nginx BSD-2-Clause, Redis BSD-3-Clause, libplebnet/libuinet BSD-2-Clause, inih BSD-3-Clause, Microthread framework GPL-2.0.
stars_or_usage: 4,265 stars. Used in production at Tencent Cloud (DNSPod authoritative DNS, HttpDNS (D+), COS access module, CDN access module), per the README.
tradeoffs: Requires DPDK + hugepages + dedicated NIC (kernel bypass), not a drop-in for arbitrary apps; Linux/FreeBSD only; adds operational complexity (core pinning, ASLR disabling); ported FreeBSD 11/13 TCP stack so feature/behavior parity with Linux netstack is not perfect
caveats: Numbers exist only in chart images. Bandwidth data labels are readable, but RPS/CPS values are approximate reads off the chart axis. The ~12x ratios are against untuned or IRQ-only-tuned kernel Nginx. Against the best-tuned kernel config the gain is ~1.46x RPS (keep-alive, 24 cores) and ~2.3x CPS (vs reuseport, 16 cores), and 3.7 KB-body bandwidth reaches parity at 40GbE line rate. Compiler, flags, load generator and client setup are not stated, and no benchmark scripts are published. Hardware and kernel (E5-2670 v3, kernel 3.10) are 2016-era. The CPS_Reuseport chart ran in a different environment. The page does not say whether kernel Nginx also returned the body directly from nginx.conf. F-Stack is not a drop-in epoll replacement: it needs DPDK NIC takeover, hugepages and dedicated busy-polling cores, and the LD_PRELOAD adapter uses ~2x CPU (per adapter/syscall/README.md). The '10M concurrent connections' claim has no supporting data. docs/F-Stack_Architecture_Layer1_System_Overview.md claims '5M RPS vs kernel 200K RPS, 25x' without a source, and the README RPS chart contradicts it (kernel Nginx si ~3.27M RPS). BSD-4-Clause and GPL-2.0 components are bundled.

name: io_uring hybrid storage I/O architecture (Oracle Database)
workload: Oracle Database 26ai (internal development build): a synthetic Update IOPS test (DBWR write-flush path), a 150 GB parallel direct-path Scan, TPC-C (5K warehouses, 210 users) and the 22-query TPC-H (1.1 TB, uncalibrated/unaudited), plus Sec 3 microbenchmarks (libaio vs six io_uring configurations on a single NVMe, block-size x device-count sweep). io_uring replaces libaio on the async batched paths; synchronous reads stay on pread.
claimed_speedup: Abstract and Table 9 (Oracle Database 26ai, 96 vCPUs, io_uring vs libaio baseline). Update IOPS (isolated DBWR write path): 1.067M to 1.428M write IOPS (+34%), CPU per physical write 58 to 41 us (-29%). Scan (150 GB, direct-path reads): CPU per read -19% at unchanged throughput. TPC-C: tpmC unchanged (2.275M vs 2.279M); server CPU 45.0% to 43.8% (-1.2 pp) only after cutting DBWR processes from 32 to 23; with the same 32 DBWR it was 45.7%. TPC-H: CPU per query -8.5% geometric mean, elapsed time within noise. Async I/O submit wait is about 75x lower. Synchronous single-block reads stay on pread (io_uring shows no gain there, and CPU/IO is about 2x higher at 512 KB-1 MB). Microbenchmark (Fig 3): geometric mean -39% CPU per I/O vs batched libaio, up to +15% IOPS in CPU-bound regimes.
compiler_and_flags: Microbenchmark artifact only: gcc -O2 -Wall -Wextra -pthread (Makefile, compiler version not stated). Build flags for the Oracle Database 26ai internal build are not stated.
hardware: End-to-end: OCI BM.DenseIO.E4 bare metal, AMD EPYC 7J13 (128 cores, 96 vCPUs given to the DB), 2 TB RAM, 8 local NVMe SSDs in software RAID-0, Oracle Linux with UEK R8. Microbenchmarks: a single NVMe device; the CPU is not stated separately.
tradeoffs: Findings are architecture/design guidance embedded in a proprietary closed-source RDBMS, not a reusable open library; benefit is workload-dependent and regresses for very large synchronous reads.
caveats: First-party benchmark by Oracle engineers of their own closed-source product; arXiv preprint submitted to PVLDB, not yet peer-reviewed. The TPC-C/TPC-H runs are unaudited and 'for internal comparison only'. Gains are almost entirely CPU efficiency, not latency or elapsed time: the TPC-C 1.2 pp CPU saving needs DBWR cut from 32 to 23, and TPC-H elapsed times are unchanged. The mechanism is the Linux io_uring interface through a custom thin layer that does not use liburing, so this is effectively io_uring-vs-libaio evidence rather than a reusable library. Artifact: github.com/rch0wdhury/iouring-rdbms-vldb-artifact (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.20099105, CC-BY-4.0 on Zenodo, no LICENSE file on GitHub, 1 star) holds only the microbenchmarks. The shared buffer registration work led to IORING_REGISTER_CLONE_BUFFERS in Linux 6.12.

name: IX (protected dataplane OS)
baseline: Linux 3.16.1 kernel TCP stack via libevent + epoll: stock memcached-1.4.18 on tuned Linux (pinned threads, IRQ affinity, tuned interrupt moderation); mTCP is a second baseline in the microbenchmarks
workload: memcached-1.4.18 ported to IX's libix event API vs stock memcached on Linux. The mutilate load generator ran Facebook ETC (20-70B keys, 1B-1KB values, 75% GET) and USR (<20B keys, 2B values, 99% GET) workloads from 23 Linux client machines over 1,476 TCP connections. Metrics are max RPS at a 500us 99th-percentile SLA and unloaded 99th-percentile latency. The paper also has NetPIPE ping-pong, short-message echo and connection-scaling (up to 250K connections) microbenchmarks.
claimed_speedup: Abstract: IX 'improves the throughput of a widely deployed, key-value store by up to 3.6x and reduces tail latency by more than 2x'. Sec 5.5 / Table 2 (memcached vs Linux): 2.8x (ETC, 550K -> 1550K RPS) and 3.6x (USR, 500K -> 1800K RPS) at a 500us 99th-percentile SLA. Unloaded 99th-percentile latency is 94 -> 45us (ETC) and 85 -> 32us (USR). Microbenchmarks: up to 10x the throughput of Linux and 1.9x of mTCP for short messages on 10GbE; one-way 64B latency 5.7us vs 24us for Linux (4x).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The 2016 code release's build files show dp/Makefile building the IX dataplane with gcc -O3 -mno-red-zone -fno-pie, and ix-bench/Makefile building its libevent/epoll client/server with gcc -O2. No compiler version is given anywhere, and no memcached build flags are given.
hardware: Server: Intel Xeon E5-2665 @ 2.4 GHz (8 cores / 16 hyperthreads per socket), 256 GB DRAM, Intel x520 10GbE NICs (82599EB), either 1 port or 4x10GbE bonded. Clients: Xeon E5-2637 @ 3.5 GHz and E5-2650 @ 2.6 GHz running Linux. Switch: Quanta/Cumulus 48x10GbE (Broadcom Trident+). OS: Ubuntu 14.04 with the Linux 3.16.1 kernel. For memcached, Linux used 8 cores and IX used 6.
tradeoffs: Research prototype OS requiring a custom kernel/dataplane split (built on the Dune hardware-virtualization mechanism); not a drop-in library and not portable to stock Linux without OS-level changes.
caveats: OSDI 2014 peer-reviewed paper. The code was released in May 2016 (ix-project/ix and ix-project/ix-bench, whose scripts cover the OSDI'14 and SoCC'15 graphs), so the released code may differ from the 2014 prototype. The paper says outright that its Linux benchmarks use 'the libevent framework with the epoll system call' and that memcached is built on libevent. The win is over the Linux kernel TCP stack plus epoll, not over the event loop alone. IX's best config used 6 cores against Linux's 8. memcached was ported to IX's libix API, and the clients ran Linux. Running IX needs VT-x (Dune), DPDK, supported Intel NICs (the README lists 82599/X520/X540) and dedicated polling hardware threads and NIC queues. License: IX's own code is the MIT text under an 'IX Open Source License' header, so GitHub reports NOASSERTION. It statically links libdune from the ix-project/dune submodule, which has no license file, and needs GPL kernel modules (dune.ko MODULE_LICENSE GPL; pcidma GPL-2.0) plus DPDK. The paper says the dataplane is 41% derived from the DPDK ixgbe driver, 26% from lwIP and 15% from Dune. There have been no commits since 2017-11-06.
found_via: USENIX OSDI 2014 presentation page https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi14/technical-sessions/presentation/belay

name: libhv
workload: pingpong echo-servers benchmark (echo-servers/benchmark.sh + pingpong_client): a single-event-loop TCP echo server per library, loaded over loopback by the libhv-based pingpong_client with 4 threads, 1000 connections, 1024-byte messages for 10s, measuring aggregate read throughput (MB/s). The CI version uses 2 threads and 100 connections.
claimed_speedup: README pingpong run (4 threads, 1000 connections, 10s, 1024-byte messages): libhv 215 MB/s vs libevent 157 MB/s (~1.37x) and libuv 156 MB/s (~1.38x); it also beats poco (165) and asio (132) and trails libev (210). Ratios derived from page data. Three GitHub Actions runs on 2026-09-25 (benchmark.yml, 2 threads, 100 connections) are consistent: libhv 115/207/120 MB/s vs libevent 79/149/81 (~1.39-1.48x) and libuv 77/125/73 (~1.49-1.66x). In those runs libhv is at parity with libev (118/212/119) and asio (118/211/115), so the README's win over asio is not reproduced.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile target echo-servers compiles each echo server and pingpong_client with -g -Wall -O3 (-std=c99 or c++11). libhv itself is built with the default BUILD_TYPE=RELEASE (-O2, -DNDEBUG). libevent, libev, libuv, asio and poco are distro packages (apt/yum/brew via echo-servers/build.sh). No compiler or library versions are given for the README run. The current CI run uses gcc 13.3.0 on ubuntu-24.04 with libevent 2.1.12, libev 4.33 and libuv 1.48.0.
hardware: Not stated for the README run. The current CI runs use GitHub-hosted ubuntu-latest (ubuntu-24.04) runners; the CPU model is not logged.
tradeoffs: Simpler, richer-protocol API than libevent/libuv/asio (built-in HTTP/WebSocket/MQTT/Redis); C core with C++ wrapper (evpp namespace, unrelated to Qihoo360/evpp)
caveats: All echo servers and the pingpong client were written by the libhv author, and the client is itself built on libhv. The baselines are simple implementations: the libuv server mallocs a buffer per read plus a write request per echo, and the libevent server allocates an evbuffer per read. The README numbers come from a 2021-03-09 run whose 4-thread/1000-connection setting was pingpong_client's default at the time; they cannot be traced to a CI run, and today's CI uses 2 threads and 100 connections. Compiler and library versions and the CPU are not stated for the README run. CI numbers swing ~1.8x between runners, though the ordering holds. The margin over libevent and libuv is modest (~1.4-1.6x), and libhv ties libev and (in current CI) asio.

name: monoio

claimed_speedup: 4-core server, 1KB messages, peak QPS: Monoio 810,075 vs Tokio (epoll) 434,565 (~1.86x, derived from page data) and vs Glommio (io_uring) 603,016 (~1.34x, derived from page data). name: picoev
workload: Re-modified version of libev's bench.c measuring per-descriptor setup time and per-event processing time across scaling file-descriptor counts, for select/epoll/kqueue backends.
claimed_speedup: README: 'it is faster than libevent or libev!' The two charts (1,000 active clients, 1k-100k fds) show picoev lowest throughout. At 100,000 fds, setup time is about 600k µs for libevent vs about 190k µs for picoev (~3x), and event-processing time is about 22.5k vs about 11k µs (~2x). libev (native) is close behind picoev (~12k µs). These values are approximate, read off the unlabeled chart axes (derived from page data).
stars_or_usage: 403 stars; vendored by the meinheld Python WSGI server (meinheld/server/picoev_*.c, ~1.45k stars)
tradeoffs: Only supports select(2)/epoll(2)/kqueue(2) (no IOCP); array-plus-bitvector-ring-buffer design gives only ~1-2s timeout granularity beyond 128 buckets; author explicitly states picoev is 'not comparable' to libevent/libev in maturity or feature set.
caveats: There is no LICENSE file. The BSD-3-Clause terms come from per-file headers (Copyright 2009 Cybozu Labs, with an unfilled '<ORGANIZATION>' placeholder), and the 326-byte declarations-only picoev_w32.h has no header. The README's chart images and original post on developer.cybozu.co.jp are dead; they survive only on web.archive.org (picoev_setup.png and picoev_event.png, 2015 snapshots). The charts have no numeric labels, and there is no stated compiler, flags, hardware, library versions or timeout settings. Only select, epoll and kqueue backends are supported, and timeouts have coarse 1-second granularity (a 128-slot ring of bit vectors). In the independent bartman/event-loop-benchmark README (5 stars, -Os -ggdb, picoev built -O2, no hardware stated), picoev's total is ~61k µs vs libevent's ~123k µs per run, with libev fastest at ~27.5k µs.

name: ringline
workload: Two-machine TCP echo benchmark (9 server configs x 4 message sizes x 4 connection counts, bare-metal Xeon, X710 40G LAG) plus a Segcache GET cache-server workload (256B/1KiB/4KiB values, 128 connections) on AWS Graviton4 c8g instances
claimed_speedup: TCP echo (Sept 2026, commit a685e16): against the best of five tokio configurations, ringline leads in 13 of 16 cells, from -10.3% to +8.9% (the page says 'roughly 0-10% faster'). It loses at 16 KiB/64 conns (-10.3%), 16 KiB/512 (-4.9%) and 4 KiB/64 (-0.1%). Against tokio's default multi-thread runtime it is +4% to +71% (256 B: +4/+70/+46/+27%; 4 KiB: +16/+57/+36/+33%; 16 KiB: +42/+71/+51%). The page itself retracts the earlier '27-71%' lead because it implied a win over tokio's best configuration. At 512 conns/256 B it does 619,863 ops/s against 591,854 for tokio-uring and 425,486 for default tokio. Segcache GET (June 2026, v0.1.3, 4 workers, 128 conns): at 256 B/1 KiB, +31%/+30% throughput, -28%/-24% p50, -15%/-18% p99, +22%/+23% ops/core-s. At 4 KiB, throughput and p50 tie, p99 is -8% and ops/core-s +14%. At open-loop saturation the two tie (NIC/PPS-bound).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 'stable' (segcache run only). Neither run gives a rustc version or build flags. The workspace has edition 2024 and MSRV 1.88, no [profile.release] overrides and no rust-toolchain pin.
hardware: Echo run: server is a 24 vCPU Xeon (hv02 guest), client a 56 vCPU Xeon (hv01 guest). The page says 'bare metal', but the runs were SystemsLab anvil-vm jobs with the X710 PFs passed through. Network is 4x Intel X710 in a direct-attached 40G LAG; no CPU model is given. 8 server workers, 16 client threads. Segcache run: AWS c8g.4xlarge (16 vCPU Graviton4, Neoverse-V2) server and c8g.8xlarge (32 vCPU Graviton4) client, same AZ, cluster placement group, Debian 13, Linux 6.12.
tradeoffs: Only ~0-10% faster than tokio's best-tuned configurations; the larger 27-71% figure holds only against tokio's default (non-per-core) config. Loses to a zero-copy tokio+splice path at 16KiB payloads. Requires manual worker-count tuning matched to concurrency for best CPU efficiency. Linux-focused (io_uring/epoll/mio backends).
caveats: First-party benchmark in the project's own repo, not independent. It stays below Tier A because the echo CPU is only 'Xeon', no rustc version or build flags are given, and the segcache harness is said to be on branch bench/fair-throughput, which no longer exists on GitHub; only the echo harness (ringline-bench) is on main. The retraction of the earlier 27-71% headline is in BENCHMARKS.md's own 'Read this first' section, not in the README. The README's Benchmarks section still describes only the June 2026 segcache run. Segcache is the only protocol-like workload. It is stale (ringline 0.1.3, June 2026), predates the harness fairness fix #392, compares against a single tokio configuration, and ties at open-loop saturation. The echo run is a byte pipe with no parsing, and its 2048-connection column is labelled directional. ringline loses to splice-based tokio at 16 KiB. The echo rig is called bare metal but was run as VM guests with NIC passthrough. The README says ringline is not a tokio replacement and is not API-compatible.

name: Seastar
workload: memaslap (libmemcached 1.0.18) GET/SET load against a Seastar-based, DPDK-backed memcached-protocol server vs stock Memcached 1.4.17 (libevent-based reactor, both multi-process and multi-threaded configurations), scaling from 2 to 20 CPU cores over a 40Gb NIC.
claimed_speedup: "SeaStar's Memcache server is 4X faster than the stock threaded memcache" and ~2x faster than the stock multi-process memcache; e.g. at 20 cores: Seastar+DPDK 4,426,457 ops/s vs stock multi-threaded 1,128,469 ops/s vs stock multi-process 2,281,064 ops/s
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon E5-2695v3 (2.3GHz base, 35MB cache, 14 cores each = 28 physical/56 HT per host), 64GB DDR4, dual Intel XL710-QDA1 40Gb NICs (hardware shared with the project's HTTPD-benchmark wiki page)
stars_or_usage: 9.4k stars; core reactor engine of ScyllaDB
tradeoffs: Requires adopting Seastar's own future/promise async model and strict shard-per-core, share-nothing design (no implicit cross-core memory sharing); its highest numbers use a DPDK kernel-bypass network stack requiring hugepages and dedicated NICs, which is not a drop-in replacement for a plain epoll/libevent deployment; native TCP stack trades standard BSD-socket compatibility for speed.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (Seastar project's own GitHub wiki), not an independent third party; the page was created and last edited Feb 19 - Mar 1, 2015 (wiki history), so it is over 11 years old; compiler and build flags are not stated (only the build/release binary path); the Seastar side runs its own userspace TCP/IP stack over DPDK kernel bypass (--network-stack native --dpdk-pmd) while stock memcached uses the Linux kernel network stack, so the gain mixes kernel bypass with the reactor design and is not an isolated reactor-vs-libevent comparison; the 4x figure is against memcached's threaded mode, which the page says suffers from lock contention (mutex_trylock busy-wait), and the page itself calls the 2x multi-process comparison 'not a fair comparison'; the multi-threaded memcached configuration is not described in the setup section; the comparison is at the whole-application (memcached) level rather than a synthetic libevent-only microbenchmark, though memcached's own event loop is libevent-based.
found_via: gh search repos --topic event-loop / gh api repos/scylladb/seastar readme -> WebFetch seastar.io (redirects/links to project wiki) -> GitHub wiki pages 'Memcached Benchmark' and 'HTTPD benchmark'

name: UCall
baseline: FastAPI/uvicorn (Python, asyncio - typically epoll-based event loop on Linux)
workload: JSON-RPC round-trip: single-client latency and 32-client throughput on AWS c7g.metal (Graviton3), Ubuntu 22.10, Linux kernel 5.19
claimed_speedup: README table: UCall io_uring (C server, connection reused) 22us / 231,000 rps vs FastAPI over REST (no connection reuse) 1,203us / 3,184 rps (~55x latency, ~72x throughput, derived from page data). Vs FastAPI over WebSocket (connection reused) 86us / 11,356 rps: ~3.9x latency, ~20x throughput (derived from page data). A closer like-for-like pair is UCall io_uring with a Python server, at 40us / 210,000 rps: ~2.2x latency and ~18x throughput vs FastAPI WebSocket (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release build with -O3 (CMakeLists.txt default). The compiler version is not stated; the reproduce steps in examples/login/README.md install g++ via apt. FastAPI/uvicorn versions are not stated.
hardware: AWS c7g.metal (Graviton 3), Ubuntu 22.10 AMI, Linux kernel 5.19; throughput clients run on the same machine as the server
tradeoffs: Cross-language comparison (C/io_uring server vs Python/ASGI client stack), so the headline numbers conflate io_uring efficiency with Python interpreter/framework overhead
caveats: Cross-language, cross-framework comparison (C or Python-bound UCall vs a Python FastAPI/uvicorn app), not a controlled event-loop shootout. The ~55x/~72x headline pairs a connection-reusing UCall server with FastAPI REST, which does not reuse connections. The like-for-like WebSocket pair gives ~3.9x latency and ~20x throughput. name: uvloop
baseline: CPython asyncio default event loop (pure-Python SelectorEventLoop, epoll-backed on Linux)
workload: Echo-server benchmark exercising asyncio's low-level socket API (loop.sock_recv/sock_sendall), high-level streams API (asyncio.start_server), and the protocol API (loop.create_server), at 1/10/100 KiB message sizes, comparing stock asyncio's default epoll-based SelectorEventLoop against uvloop (a libuv-backed loop swapped in via asyncio.set_event_loop_policy).
claimed_speedup: README states 'uvloop makes asyncio 2-4x faster'. Read off the README bar chart (derived from page data): protocol API at 1 KiB ~106k uvloop vs ~43k asyncio req/s (~2.5x); sockets API at 1 KiB ~52k vs ~13.5k (~3.9x); streams API at 1 KiB ~44k vs ~17.5k (~2.5x); at 100 KiB the gap narrows to ~1.8x (protocol, ~23.5k vs ~12.8k) and ~1.4x (streams, ~12k vs ~8.8k).

tradeoffs: Adds a compiled C-extension (Cython + vendored libuv) build/install dependency instead of the pure-Python stdlib loop; historically Linux/macOS-focused with weaker Windows story; some asyncio edge cases (e.g. certain subprocess/signal behaviors) have lagged the stdlib implementation over time.
caveats: First-party benchmark. The chart was committed on 2016-05-22 and the linked magic.io blog post (May 3, 2016) no longer resolves live; it is still readable via the Wayback Machine (2017-03-01 snapshot), which gives the CPU, OS, Python 3.5 and vmbench setup but no compiler or flags. At 100 KiB messages the gain is only ~1.4-1.8x, below the '2-4x' headline. Both loops ultimately use epoll on Linux (uvloop through libuv), so this is a Python-event-loop-implementation comparison rather than a win over raw epoll. name: iohttpparser (stateful-strict/lenient profiles)
workload: req/s, MiB/s and ns/req for 22 fixed scenarios: 21 common request, response and header-stress fixtures of 33-703 bytes, plus one 99-byte CONNECT request. Each timed iteration parses one complete single-message buffer from scratch. Every call re-initializes the parser: llhttp_init plus llhttp_finish, or a fresh ihtp state for the stateful profiles. Each run does 200,000 iterations after 1,000 warmups, and the reported figure is the median of 5 runs. The comparison covers four iohttpparser profiles against vendored picohttpparser and llhttp 9.3.1 (bench/bench_throughput_compare.c).
claimed_speedup: summary.md median req/s, 22 scenarios (21 common + 1 CONNECT). The best iohttpparser profile (stateful-strict alone gives the same count) beats llhttp in 16 and loses in 6. Wins include: req-headers 9.12M vs 7.87M (stateful-strict, 1.16x); resp-headers 12.08M vs 9.55M (stateful-lenient, 1.26x); hdr-value-ascii-clean 7.72M vs 5.16M (1.50x); hdr-count-32-minimal 2.89M vs 1.93M (1.50x); req-connect 14.32M vs 11.36M (1.26x). All ratios are derived from page data. llhttp wins req-small (22.91M vs best 18.36M, 0.80x), req-line-only, req-line-connect, hdr-name-heavy, hdr-uncommon-valid and hdr-count-04-minimal. picohttpparser is fastest in 21 of 22 scenarios. The exception is hdr-count-32-minimal, where stateful-strict edges it (2.89M vs 2.86M req/s).
compiler_and_flags: clang 22.1.0, CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release with CMAKE_INTERPROCEDURAL_OPTIMIZATION=ON, -fuse-ld=lld -flto=thin (clang-release CMake preset)
hardware: KVM guest with a generic QEMU 'AMD EPYC Processor' vCPU (family 23 model 1 stepping 2), 8 vCPU, 8 MiB L3; host CPU SKU not stated (per host.txt lscpu)
tradeoffs: Pull-based API with explicit parser state and a separate semantics/body-decoder stage, unlike llhttp's callback-driven model; adds framing-ambiguity rejection (TE+CL, conflicting Content-Length) that llhttp only partially covers; consistently slower than picohttpparser across all measured scenarios.
caveats: Zero-star, single-contributor project published in March 2026, with no independent adoption or third-party reproduction. The benchmark ran in a KVM guest whose lscpu shows only the generic 'AMD EPYC Processor' vCPU model, so the real host CPU is unknown and results carry shared-cloud noise. Each iteration parses one tiny (33-703 byte) standalone message with per-call parser init, which measures small-message latency rather than streaming throughput. Wins over llhttp are not uniform: llhttp wins 6 of 22 scenarios, including req-small (0.80x), three request-line cases and three header cases. picohttpparser is 1.07-2.46x faster than the best iohttpparser profile in 21 of 22 scenarios.

name: http.c3l
workload: pico's own benchmark request (request line + headers, no body) parsed in a tight loop on one pinned core, comparing http::parser's callback-driven and callback-free ("no cb") streaming request parser against vendored picohttpparser
claimed_speedup: Typical (rounded) result on the bench page: the "no cb" run at ~99 ns/req (~10.1M req/s, ~113% of pico) vs picohttpparser at ~112 ns/req (~8.9M req/s), about 13% faster; the full callback-driven http::parser is at parity (~112 ns/req, ~99% of pico's throughput). In bench/bench.c3 the "no cb" run registers no callbacks at all (empty Settings, null context), so it extracts no method/path/header data while pico fills its method/path and 32-entry header array; the equal-output comparison is therefore parity, not a win. The page also says the SSE2 path is ~1.5x faster than pico's scalar (non-SSE4.2) build, with no numbers table for that claim
compiler_and_flags: c3c build at O3 (c3c version not stated); vendored picohttpparser compiled as a c-source of the same bench project with cflags -O3 -msse4.2 (C compiler not stated); http::parser uses 16-byte char[<16>] vectors (SSE2 on x86-64, NEON on aarch64 per README/src/simd.c3), no -march=native
hardware: "x86-64" only; exact CPU model not stated; author pins to one core with taskset
tradeoffs: http::parser is a sans-IO streaming push parser (callback per token, consume/re-present contract) vs picohttpparser's one-shot whole-buffer parse into caller arrays; the streaming design is what costs the ~10-15% callback overhead; written in C3, a young C-like systems language, not C or C++ directly (interoperable via C ABI)
caveats: Author's own bench README frames this as "indicative, not a verdict" given the different parser shapes (streaming push parser with per-token callbacks vs one-shot array filling) and also notes http::parser does extra body-framing work; the only faster number (~13%) comes from a run with no callbacks registered, which delivers no parsed fields while pico fills its header array, so at equal output the usable callback-driven parser is only at parity (~99% of pico); figures are rounded "typical" values from a single fixed hot-cache request, no raw output, no CPU model or compiler versions; repo history shows a single commit (authored 2026-06-27, committed 2026-08-02)

name: httpp
workload: Single-threaded repeated parse of picohttpparser's own classic sample GET request (image request with UA/cookie headers), 10,000,000 iterations x 5 runs, averaged.
claimed_speedup: At -O3: httppv2 (2.0.0) 8,893,776.12 req/s (1.124382s) vs picohttpparser 3,939,350.39 req/s (2.538490s), ~2.26x (derived from page data); httppv1 (1.0.0) 2,855,841.74 req/s (3.501595s), slower than pico at -O3. At -O0: httppv1 2,008,030.68 and httppv2 3,475,424.44 req/s vs picohttpparser 1,130,465.28 req/s.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 15.2.1 20251112; -O0 and -O3 only, no -march/-msse4.2 (benchmarks/run.sh), so picohttpparser's SSE4.2 fast path is not compiled in; picohttpparser is cloned unpinned from h2o master at run time
hardware: Ryzen 7, ~4.79GHz peak frequency (exact SKU not given)
tradeoffs: Header-only C, fixed-size stack-allocated header array, no SIMD (wins via lower per-call overhead, not vectorization). Only the v2.0.0 variant beats picohttpparser at -O3; v1.0.0 is slower at -O3 despite winning at -O0.
caveats: CPU given only as 'Ryzen 7' (no SKU); first-party benchmark, 5 runs averaged, clock()-based timing. The comparison is not like-for-like: picohttpparser runs its scalar path (no -msse4.2) while httpp calls libc memchr/strstr, which are SIMD in glibc. httpp also does far less validation: no token/CTL character checks on method, path or header names/values, no incomplete-request (-2) handling, and strstr over the input assumes NUL-termination. httpp is header-only and inlined into the bench TU, while pico is a separate TU. The -O0 rows are debug builds and should be ignored. Very new single-maintainer project (9 stars).

Header parsing (README table, pkg/header/parser_bench_test.go): Simple GET (1 header) 252 ns/0 allocs vs fasthttp 1,336 ns/1 alloc = 5.3x; Typical (8 headers) 2,377 vs 6,198 ns = 2.6x; Many headers (20) 4,776 vs 10,077 ns = 2.1x. name: fasthttp (Go HTTP server/client package)
workload: Go testing benchmarks (server_timing_test.go, client_timing_test.go; go test -bench -benchmem -benchtime=10s) at GOMAXPROCS=1 and 4. Server tests send a GET that gets a small fake response over an in-memory fake listener and connections, with no real network. They cover 1/2/10/10K requests per connection, and 1/2/10/100 requests per connection with 10K clients, comparing fasthttp.Server with net/http's http.Server. Client tests run an end-to-end GET over TCP (1/10/100 conns) and in-memory (1-1000 conns; fasthttp also 10K).
claimed_speedup: README: 'fasthttp server is up to 6 times faster than net/http' and 'fasthttp client is up to 4 times faster'. The 'up to 10x' is the GitHub repo description, not the README. The same case at GOMAXPROCS=1 is 7151 vs 1422 ns/op, about 5.0x. The best server row is 14010 vs 2208 ns/op, about 6.3x (GOMAXPROCS=1, 2 reqs/conn, 10K clients). Client end-to-end is about 2.0-2.3x over TCP and 4.9-11.7x in-memory, peaking at 31010 vs 2645 ns/op with 1000 in-memory conns at GOMAXPROCS=4. All ratios are derived from page data.

name: hparse
workload: poop (like hyperfine, but with hardware counters; bench.txt comes from `poop -d 10000`) runs standalone binaries for picohttpparser (C), httparse (Rust) and hparse (Zig). Each binary parses one fixed 430-byte HTTP/1.1 GET request with 9 headers into a 32-slot header array, 10,000,000 times. Metrics: wall time, peak RSS, CPU cycles, instructions retired, cache references and misses, branch misses.
claimed_speedup: hparse: 1.27s wall-time / 5.38G cpu_cycles / 8.01G instructions vs picohttpparser: 1.45s wall-time / 6.16G cpu_cycles / 34.7G instructions (~12.5% faster wall-clock, ~12.6% fewer cycles, ~77% fewer instructions retired); also beats httparse (Rust) at 1.54s wall-time / 6.53G cycles.
compiler_and_flags: hparse: zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast (bench/hparse/build.zig uses standardTargetOptions, so the default target is the native CPU). httparse 1.10.0: cargo build --release with [profile.release] opt-level=3 and no target-cpu. picohttpparser: bench/picohttpparser/Makefile runs `gcc ./main.c ./picohttpparser.c -I. -O3` on a vendored copy, with no -msse4.2 or -march flag, not the upstream Makefile. No compiler versions are stated.
hardware: Unspecified x86-64 (AMD64) Linux machine, according to the maintainer's comment in PR #2. No CPU model is stated for the bench.txt run.
tradeoffs: Zig-only public API (needs a C shim for direct C++ linkage); streaming/never-allocates design explicitly modeled after picohttpparser so it can be 'swapped in smoothly'. A separate skylake-tuned build target exists (-Dcpu=skylake) but its numbers are not published.
caveats: 1) No CPU model or compiler versions are given for the bench.txt run (it only says AMD64 Linux, in PR #2), so it is capped at C. 2) The baseline build is not like-for-like. picohttpparser is compiled with plain `gcc -O3` and no -msse4.2 or -march, so its `#ifdef __SSE4_2__` fast path is probably compiled out on a default x86-64 GCC. It retires about 3470 instructions per parse, roughly 8 per byte (derived from page data), which is consistent with the scalar path. hparse is built for the native CPU. 3) The win depends on the platform. On Apple Silicon, hparse is slower than picohttpparser. The maintainer's open issue #3 shows M4 Pro hyperfine times of hparse 1.464s vs picohttpparser 0.965s vs httparse 0.753s, and PR #2 on an M3 shows hparse 2.015s vs picohttpparser 1.252s. 4) A third party reproduced the x86 result in PR #2 on an AMD Ryzen 7 8745HS: hparse 1.01s vs picohttpparser 1.14s wall time (-11.3%), 4.91G vs 5.54G cycles. 5) This is a microbenchmark that repeats one request from a single host. 12.5% less wall time is about 1.14x faster (derived from page data).

workload: Single-process, interleaved A/B/C loop, 12 rounds x 4 reps over a urls.txt corpus. Each op parses one URL and reads protocol, host, path (abspath / get_pathname), query and fragment. name: httparse (Rust push parser for HTTP/1.x)
workload: Rust nightly #[bench] with [profile.bench] lto=true (benches/parse.rs at v1.3.0). It parses one fixed ~700-byte, 10-header browser GET request (the 'hello-kitty-darth-vader' request) and one 3-line short request. picohttpparser is called over FFI through the pico-sys 0.0.1 crate.
claimed_speedup: PR #40 (maintainer, rustc 1.27; pico built via pico-sys without SSE4.2): with -C target_cpu=native, httparse 405 ns vs pico 492 ns on the full browser request, ~1.21x (derived from page data), and 62 vs 72 ns on the short request, ~1.16x (derived). With runtime SIMD detection: 451 vs 492 ns, ~1.09x (derived), and 70 vs 72 ns. With SIMD off, httparse is slower on the full request (529 vs 492 ns) and faster only on the short one (66 vs 72 ns). The maintainer's summary: 'Without SIMD, httparse is oh-so-slightly faster than Pico when the requests are tiny, but a bit slower on a more realist request from a browser.' The record's 'faster than picohttpparser, when SIMD is not available' (lib.rs doc v1.2.3-v1.2.5, removed in v1.3.0) never came with numbers, and PR #40 contradicts it for realistic requests.
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.27 (nightly bench harness), [profile.bench] lto=true; runs with SIMD off, with runtime SSE4.2/AVX2 detection, and with -C target_cpu=native. pico-sys compiles picohttpparser.c through the gcc crate with no -msse4.2, so pico runs its non-SSE4.2 path.
stars_or_usage: 714 GitHub stars; ~742M crates.io downloads (~169M recent); the de facto HTTP/1.x parser for Rust (hyper, actix-web and most of the Rust HTTP ecosystem)
tradeoffs: no_std-friendly, allocation-free, push-style API (caller supplies header-slot buffer); safety-critical `unsafe` is scoped to a single submodule; the historical picohttpparser claim is explicitly qualified to only the no-SIMD case, which is increasingly rare since SIMD paths are now auto-detected at runtime.
caveats: The only measured wins over picohttpparser pit httparse's SIMD paths against pico built without SSE4.2 (pico-sys uses default cc flags). Issue #85 (2021, still open) says this is not apples to apples, and the maintainer replied 'good point'. With pico built with -msse4 plus cross-language LTO, a third-party user reported pico at ~2900 MB/s vs httparse at 1751 MB/s (text in issue #85, full tables only as images). With both parsers' SIMD off, the maintainer's own PR #40 shows httparse slower on the realistic request (529 vs 492 ns) and ahead only on a tiny request (66 vs 72 ns). The 2018 contributor PR #38 shows it slower on both without SIMD (468 vs 405 ns, 54 vs 53 ns). No CPU model is given anywhere, and the numbers date from 2018. PR #112 (2022) removed the pico targets from benches, so current code no longer compares against picohttpparser. The out-of-the-box edge is real but fragile: httparse's runtime SIMD detection beats a generically built pico by ~1.09x on the full request.
found_via: gh search code "faster than picohttpparser" -> vendored copies of httparse 1.2.3 src/lib.rs (e.g. mfarrugi/cargo-raze-example-stdx); verified against current seanmonstar/httparse source

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from D. The record had no numbers page, but the maintainer's merged PR #40 (2018-06-22) has `cargo bench` results for httparse vs picohttpparser. The bench code is public (benches/parse.rs at v1.3.0, pico via the pico-sys crate) and the rustc version (1.27) and RUSTFLAGS are stated, but no CPU model is given (only 'my CPU has SSE4.2'). That is first-party C, not A.
verification.notes: The record's claim sentence is real (lib.rs doc in 1.2.3-1.2.5; v1.0-1.2.0 said '1.6 times slower than pico'), but the project's own later numbers contradict it for realistic requests. I kept the entry at C on PR #40, whose SIMD httparse beats non-SSE4.2 pico by 1.09-1.21x, and flagged the unfair-baseline issue (#85). If the orchestrator wants fair-baseline evidence only, this is a reject candidate ('not-faster'), because the only fair-build report has pico ~1.66x faster. Metadata checks out: MIT OR Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-06-30, not a fork, not archived.

name: ls-hpack (LiteSpeed HPACK)
baseline: nghttp2 (HPACK); the numeric benchmark covers only nghttp2's HPACK Huffman encoder (nghttp2_hd_huffman.c at revision 0e1d0400d86a)
workload: HPACK Huffman string encoding microbenchmark (RFC 7541 Huffman code). Code extracted from each project into litespeedtech/benchmarks/huffman-encoder and run for a fixed iteration count on 4 inputs: 'LiteSpeed' (small), a real x-fb-debug header value from the Facebook response QIF (medium), the same value with backslashes to force the fallback path, and several paragraphs of prose (large). Median of 5 runs. The companion decoder benchmark compares only against nginx 1.16.1's Huffman decoder.
claimed_speedup: ls-hpack's fast Huffman encoder vs nghttp2's encoder, in seconds (median of 5): 'LiteSpeed' 8.67 vs 20.59 (2.37x), x-fb-debug 5.25 vs 30.31 (5.77x), x-fb-backslash 7.22 vs 32.21 (4.46x), idle text 9.32 vs 52.25 (5.61x). The same post also has it 1.11x-2.12x faster than nginx's encoder and 1.18x-3.59x faster than h2o's. The companion 'Fast Huffman Decoder' post (2019-09-16) reports 1.15x-1.96x faster than nginx 1.16.1's decoder, which it says derives from nghttp2's 4-bit decoder. Bun's build script separately says ls-hpack is "faster than nghttp2's for our workloads", with no numbers.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile CFLAGS=-Wall -DNDEBUG -O3 -g0; compiler and version not stated
stars_or_usage: 56 stars; vendored by oven-sh/bun (scripts/build/deps/lshpack.ts) and a git submodule of litespeedtech/lsquic (1,876 stars); used in LiteSpeed Web Server
tradeoffs: depends on xxhash at runtime; library itself ships no benchmark suite or numbers, so the speed claim is entirely third-party and unverified from ls-hpack's own repo
caveats: The only numbers are first-party (LiteSpeed blog, 2019) and cover the HPACK Huffman encoder component only, not full HPACK encode/decode against nghttp2's HPACK API. Each project's code was extracted into standalone C files, and the nghttp2 copy is a 2019 revision (0e1d0400d86a), so current nghttp2 may differ. No CPU model or compiler version is stated. The litespeedtech/benchmarks repo has no license file (the benchmark harness only; ls-hpack itself is MIT). The decoder benchmark compares only against nginx's decoder, not nghttp2's. Bun's adoption comment gives no numbers.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than nghttp2" surfaced oven-sh/bun:scripts/build/deps/lshpack.ts (and several Bun forks with the same vendored comment)

verification.tier_reason: Upgraded from D. LiteSpeed's own 'Fast Huffman Encoder' post (2019-10-03) publishes median timings of ls-hpack's HPACK Huffman encoder against nghttp2's, nginx's and h2o's. The code is public in litespeedtech/benchmarks/huffman-encoder (comp-enc driver, bench.pl, Makefile CFLAGS -O3 -DNDEBUG -g0), but the post gives no CPU model and no compiler version, so it is first-party C, not A.
verification.notes: benchmark_url was null. A brief search of LiteSpeed's blog and repos found real numbers against nghttp2 (the Huffman encoder post plus its public harness in litespeedtech/benchmarks), so benchmark_url is corrected and the tier goes from D to C. page_compares_against_baseline and numbers_found_on_page refer to that corrected URL. The record's 'metric: other' could reasonably become 'throughput' (time for a fixed iteration count), but metric is not a correctable field.

name: Sogou C++ Workflow (HTTP Server)
workload: Minimal HTTP server returning a fixed random ASCII body (with Date/Content-Type headers); concurrency doubled over 1-2048 and body size doubled over 16B-64KB (orthogonal), load from wrk/wrk2 on a separate machine. workflow ran 16 poller + 20 handler threads; nginx 40 worker processes; brpc 40 threads. A second test measured latency CDFs vs brpc only (concurrency 1024, 1KB bodies, 20K/100K/200K QPS with 1% 5ms slow requests).
claimed_speedup: Read off the docs/benchmark.md charts (derived from page data). QPS vs concurrency (benchmark-01.png): at concurrency 256-2048, workflow ~490-530K QPS vs nginx ~203-213K for 64B/512B bodies (~2.3-2.6x) and ~442-458K vs ~180-205K for 4096B (~2.2-2.5x); the gap is small at concurrency 1-4, where brpc leads. QPS vs body length (benchmark-02.png): workflow ~425-545K vs nginx ~165-220K up to 4KB, but at 8-16KB the workflow-512 and nginx-512 curves nearly meet (~202K vs ~195K; ~166K vs ~163K) and at 32KB/64KB all servers converge at ~88K/~45K. Latency: at fixed body size workflow is lower than nginx as concurrency grows (~4.0-4.5ms vs ~12.4-14.1ms at concurrency 2048), but at concurrency 512 with 16KB/32KB bodies workflow latency (~8ms/~18ms) is higher than nginx (~4ms/~9ms) (benchmark-04.png). The prose states only that workflow 'can maintain 500K QPS' for 64B and 512B bodies at sufficient concurrency and that it beats brpc and nginx throughout the QPS curves.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.8.5 stated on the page; optimization flags are not stated. benchmark/CMakeLists.txt (initial 2020 commit) defaults to CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE RelWithDebInfo with -Wall -fPIC -pipe -std=c++11 -fno-exceptions. nginx and brpc build options are not stated.
hardware: Two identical machines (server and client, ~0.1ms RTT): Intel Xeon E5-2630 v4 @ 2.20GHz, '40 Cores' x86_64 (socket count not stated), 192GB RAM, 25000Mbps NIC, CentOS 7.8.2003, kernel 3.10.0-1127.el7.x86_64
tradeoffs: Task/series-based async programming model has a learning curve vs simple thread-per-request servers.
caveats: First-party benchmark from the 2020 docs (GCC 4.8.5, kernel 3.10). Results are PNG charts; only the ~500K QPS figure is in prose, and the page says only selected concurrency/length combinations are plotted. nginx config and brpc server code are not published, and their tuning (40 workers/threads) was chosen by the workflow authors. The advantage over nginx vanishes at large bodies: QPS converges at 16-64KB (likely bandwidth-bound on the 25Gbps NIC), and at concurrency 512 with 16KB/32KB bodies workflow latency is higher than nginx. brpc is slightly ahead at concurrency 1-4 and at 20K QPS in the latency CDF.
found_via: GitHub: gh api repos/sogou/workflow/contents/docs -> docs/benchmark.md

verification.tier_reason: First-party docs/benchmark.md states the CPU (Xeon E5-2630 v4 @ 2.20GHz, 40 cores), GCC 4.8.5, NIC and OS, and the workflow server code is public (benchmark/benchmark-01-http_server.cc). Optimization flags are not stated on the page (only implied by the RelWithDebInfo default in benchmark/CMakeLists.txt), and the nginx config and brpc server code are not published, so the baseline side is not reproducible and it is not A; first-party, so not B.
verification.notes: Real entry with a genuine nginx comparison, but tier A was too high (flags unstated on page, baseline configs unpublished) and 'consistently better across all combinations' is overstated: the charts show convergence at 16-64KB bodies and worse latency than nginx at 16/32KB, concurrency 512. Metadata verified: Apache-2.0, not a fork, not archived, 14,424 stars, last commit 2026-08-10 (active).

name: Agoo-C
workload: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks run of 2026-09-24: `zrk --plain --closed` (closed loop over keep-alive connections, not oha), 15 s at each concurrency level 64/256/512. Each headline number is the average over the routes in .env (GET /, GET /user/0, POST /user; SQL avg in .tasks/db.rake), all hello-world handlers. The framework container is pinned to cores 0-3 (SERVER_CPUS) and the load generator to cores 4-15.
claimed_speedup: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks data.json of 2026-09-24 (develop branch, commit f673364): agoo-c 0.7 (release v0.7.3) 74,974 / 141,394 / 149,193 req/s at concurrency 64 / 256 / 512 vs Go net/http ('nethttp', label 1.22) 71,499 / 67,382 / 67,239 req/s, i.e. 1.05x / 2.10x / 2.22x (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: debian:trixie-slim + build-essential (Debian trixie default GCC is 14.2; the suite does not print the version). libagoo v0.7.3 is built with a plain `cd agoo-c/src && make`, which without build=release selects the debug flags `-g -Og -std=gnu11` (agoo-c src/Makefile). The benchmark app simple.c is compiled with `-O3 -std=gnu11` (c/agoo-c/Makefile). Go side: golang:1.27 image, `go build -trimpath`, GOAMD64=v3.
hardware: Single shared host per data.json: 16 CPUs (Etc.nprocessors), Linux 7.2.6-200.fc44.x86_64. The cpu_name 'M1 Eight-Core Processor' and memory 7,733,008 kB are hardcoded in .tasks/db.rake, not measured, so the CPU model is unknown; a comment in go/Dockerfile names an AMD Ryzen 7 5700U, not confirmed for this run. Server container limited to 4 cores (SERVER_CPUS=0-3), load generator on cores 4-15.
tradeoffs: Unmaintained since ~2020; C API only, so C++ use requires wrapping; only roughly ties Go net/http at the lowest tested concurrency.
caveats: Single suite run: data.json is overwritten on every run, and the suite says results from different method revisions are not comparable. At concurrency 64 agoo-c's server_cpu_saturation was only 0.58 (2.34 of 4 cores), below the suite's 75% server-bound threshold, so the c=64 figure is not a clean framework number; at 256/512 it was 0.99. Earlier snapshots vary widely. Master data.json of 2026-09-20 (older zrk method, no core pinning) shows 95,173 / 124,024 / 114,466 vs nethttp 96,149 / 85,406 / 83,964 req/s (0.99x / 1.45x / 1.36x). Under the pre-September oha method (a new connection per request, June-August 2026) agoo-c recorded only ~1.3-2.0K req/s vs nethttp ~2.1-26K, so it was slower there. The suite builds libagoo in its default debug mode (-g -Og), which likely understates agoo-c. The tested release v0.7.3 dates from 2019-11-10, and there are no commits since 2020-12-16.
