name: eRPC
baseline: NSDI'19 paper baselines: FaSST RPCs and raw RDMA reads/writes (measured; eRPC is comparable but slightly slower), IX (per-core RPC rate quoted from the IX paper), NetChain and ZabFPGA replication (their published numbers), and the Cell RDMA B-tree (published numbers). The paper never benchmarks kernel TCP/UDP socket RPC or HERD.
workload: Small (32-byte) and large (8MB) RPC calls over Ethernet/InfiniBand/RoCE NICs, plus a 3-way Raft replication port, on commodity DPDK-capable or Mellanox NICs
claimed_speedup: NSDI'19 paper: one core handles ~10M small RPCs/s vs ~1.5M 64 B RPCs/s with IX (IX figure quoted, not re-measured; ~6.7x derived from page data). 3-way Raft replication takes 5.5 us median vs NetChain's published 9.7 us (~1.8x, derived from page data) and is 3% slower than ZabFPGA at the leader (3.1 vs 3.0 us). Masstree-over-eRPC median GET is 2.7 us, 'around 10x faster' than Cell's RDMA B-tree. Against its measured RDMA baselines eRPC is slightly slower: per-thread small-RPC rate up to 18% below FaSST, median latency up to 800 ns above RDMA reads, and at least 70% of RDMA-write bandwidth for requests of 32 kB or more (75 Gbps peak on one core). The README's absolute figures (2.3 us RTT, ~10M RPCs/s per core, 60-80M RPCs/s per NIC, 75 Gbps, 5.3 us Raft) have no baseline on that page. The paper gives 5.5 us, not 5.3 us, for Raft and does not contain the 60-80M per NIC figure.
compiler_and_flags: The paper does not state them. The repo's CMakeLists.txt with the default PERF=ON uses CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE RelWithDebInfo plus -std=c++11 -march=native. The compiler is not named.
hardware: NSDI'19 Table 1 lists three clusters. CX3: 11 nodes, 56 Gbps ConnectX-3 InfiniBand, Intel Xeon E5-2650 (8 cores). CX4: 100 CloudLab nodes, 25 GbE ConnectX-4 Lx lossy Ethernet, Xeon E5-2640 v4 (10 cores). CX5: 8 nodes, dual-port 40 GbE ConnectX-5, Xeon E5-2697 v3 (14 cores) or E5-2683 v4 (16 cores). Large-RPC bandwidth was measured between two CX5 nodes over 100 Gbps ConnectX-5 InfiniBand.
tradeoffs: Requires DPDK/RDMA-capable NICs and huge pages; a binary RPC library, not an HTTP-semantics server (no TLS/HTTP parsing); app must integrate its session/event-loop model
caveats: The paper's thesis is that eRPC is comparable to specialized systems while staying general. It never measures kernel TCP/UDP socket RPC or HERD, and against FaSST and raw RDMA it is slightly slower. Its 'faster' comparisons (IX, NetChain, Cell, and FaRM at scale) use numbers from other papers on different hardware; the authors say the NetChain comparison 'must be taken with a grain of salt'. The category fit is datacenter RPC over DPDK/RDMA rather than HTTP serving. The README's 5.3 us Raft and 60-80M RPCs/s per NIC figures are not in the paper, which gives 5.5 us. Authors now point new users to microsoft/machnet. The LICENSE file is the Apache-2.0 notice header (GitHub reports NOASSERTION).
found_via: arXiv/USENIX query 'eRPC general purpose RPC library' -> https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi19/presentation/kalia and https://www.usenix.org/system/files/nsdi19-kalia.pdf

verification.tier_reason: The README at benchmark_url lists only absolute figures with no baseline. The linked peer-reviewed NSDI'19 paper does make comparative claims, but mostly against numbers published in other papers: ~10M vs ~1.5M 64 B RPCs/s per core against IX (quoted), 5.5 vs 9.7 us Raft replication against NetChain (published), and ~10x lower GET latency than Cell. The benchmark code (apps/small_rpc_tput, apps/large_rpc_tput, apps/latency, apps/smr) runs only eRPC, and the compiler is never named, so it cannot be A. Tier B is kept, but the win comes from comparisons across papers.
verification.notes: Metadata checked with gh: Apache-2.0 per the LICENSE file, not archived, not a fork, 907 stars, last commit 2024-05-09, so stale is correct. Tier stays B, but the verdict is downgrade because the record's baseline (kernel TCP/UDP RPC, FaSST/HERD) misstates the paper: it never benchmarks kernel sockets or HERD, and eRPC loses slightly to FaSST.

corrected_fields.baseline: conventional kernel TCP/UDP socket-based RPC (and specialized RDMA-only systems like FaSST/HERD)
corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: up to 10 million 32-byte RPCs/sec on one CPU core (60-80M RPCs/sec per NIC); 75 Gbps on one connection for 8MB RPCs; 2.3us round-trip RPC latency over UDP/Ethernet; 5.3us for 3-way Raft replication
corrected_fields.hardware: Mellanox CX3-CX5 or DPDK-capable NICs (exact CPU model not stated on the pages opened this session; full details are in the NSDI'19 paper PDF, which could not be text-extracted via WebFetch)
corrected_fields.caveats: NSDI'19 paper's own baseline is conventional TCP/UDP RPC and other specialized RDMA systems, not nginx/Boost.Beast/actix-web/uvloop directly, so baseline_in_list=false; exact hardware CPU model and compiler flags could not be confirmed from the pages opened (WebFetch could not extract readable text from the PDF); category fit is RPC-over-network rather than literal HTTP serving, included because the assignment's own starting query explicitly targets kernel-bypass high-performance server research. Authors now point new users to a successor project, microsoft/machnet, for DPDK-based messaging (checked; 162 stars, MIT, active, but its README states only an absolute number '750K RPS at 61us P99.9' with no named baseline comparison, so it does not itself qualify under rule 1).

name: FlexTOE
baseline: Linux host TCP stack, TAS (TCP Acceleration as an OS Service), and the Chelsio Terminator hardware TCP offload engine
workload: Memcached and RPC microbenchmarks on an Agilio-CX40 SmartNIC, plus single-connection RPC throughput on x86 and BlueField hosts
claimed_speedup: From the abstract, arXiv 2110.10919 and NSDI'22 alike: Memcached scales up to 38% better than TAS and saves up to 81% of host CPU cycles vs Chelsio. 99.99th-percentile RPC RTT is 3.2x lower than Chelsio and 50% lower than TAS. Single-connection RPC throughput is up to 2.4x TAS on x86 and 4x TAS on BlueField. The full paper's Linux-kernel-TCP figures: Memcached throughput up to 5.5x Linux, 4.9x Chelsio and 1.6x TAS (Fig. 8). RPC throughput at 250 cycles/RPC is up to 4x Linux and 5.3x Chelsio when receiving, and over 7.6x Linux and Chelsio when sending (Fig. 10). With up to 2K connections it reaches 3.3x Linux. FlexTOE loses in some cases: median small-RPC latency is 20 us vs 14 us for Chelsio and 16 us for TAS, and TAS is 1.5x better in the connection-scalability benchmark.
compiler_and_flags: SmartNIC firmware was built with the NFP compiler toolchain 6.1.0.1. The host compiler and flags are not stated.
hardware: Two 20-core Intel Xeon Gold 6138 @ 2 GHz servers (40 GB RAM), each with a Netronome Agilio CX40 40 Gbps, a Chelsio Terminator T62100-LP-CR 100 Gbps and an Intel XL710 40 Gbps NIC. Extra clients: two 2x18-core Xeon Gold 6154 @ 3 GHz (ConnectX-5 100 Gbps) and two 4-core Xeon E3-1230 v5 @ 3.4 GHz (82599ES 10 Gbps), on a 100 Gbps switch. The generalization runs used a Mellanox BlueField MBF1M332A-ASCAT 25 Gbps SmartNIC and a 32-core AMD EPYC 7452 @ 2.35 GHz host with a ConnectX-5 100 Gbps NIC.
tradeoffs: Requires a Netronome Agilio SmartNIC; programmability via C/eBPF/XDP adds development complexity vs. a plain sockets server; unmaintained since 2022
caveats: FlexTOE needs a Netronome Agilio (NFP-4000/6000) SmartNIC and 1G hugepages; the x86 and BlueField ports are described in the paper's appendix E but no separate port or benchmark directory is visible in the repo tree. It trades median latency for tail latency and throughput (20 us median vs 14-16 us for Chelsio/TAS), and TAS beats it by 1.5x on connection scalability. TAS ran on an Intel XL710 because of a slow Agilio DPDK driver. The category fit is a TCP offload engine rather than an HTTP server. The TAS baseline is an academic stack; the Linux kernel TCP stack is the recognizable incumbent (up to 5.5x Memcached throughput).
found_via: arXiv query 'TAS TCP Acceleration OS Service Kaufmann' -> https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.10919 (FlexTOE: Flexible TCP Offload with Fine-Grained Parallelism)

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed NSDI'22 paper measures FlexTOE head-to-head against the Linux kernel TCP stack, TAS and the Chelsio T6 TOE on the same testbed (Xeon Gold 6138 hosts) and shows wins. It is not A: the repo has no benchmark code (no memtier/RPC benchmark directory) and the host compiler and flags are never stated (only 'NFP compiler toolchain 6.1.0.1' for the SmartNIC firmware).
verification.notes: The abstract numbers are exact on arXiv and in the NSDI'22 PDF (both opened). benchmark_url now points at the full NSDI PDF, which also holds the Linux-baseline figures. gh confirms BSD-3-Clause, not archived, not a fork, 62 stars, last commit 2022-02-27, so abandoned is correct.

corrected_fields.claimed_speedup: Per the paper's own abstract: Memcached scales up to 38% better on FlexTOE than on TAS; saves up to 81% of host CPU cycles vs. Chelsio; cuts 99.99th-percentile RPC RTT by 3.2x vs. Chelsio and by 50% vs. TAS; improves single-connection RPC throughput up to 2.4x on x86 and 4x on BlueField
corrected_fields.hardware: Netronome Agilio-CX40 SmartNIC; x86 and BlueField hosts (exact host CPU model not stated in the abstract)
corrected_fields.caveats: One of its named baselines, TAS (tcp-acceleration-service/tas), is itself unreleased since 2020 and its EuroSys'19 paper page returned HTTP 403 (ACM DL) this session, so TAS's own standalone claims could not be independently verified and TAS is not reported as its own entry; FlexTOE's numbers above come from its own arXiv preprint abstract (peer-reviewed at NSDI'22), which is openly accessible, but exact host CPU model and compiler flags are not stated there

name: Shenango
baseline: ZygOS (a state-of-the-art kernel-bypass network stack) and standard Linux kernel networking
workload: memcached 1.5.6 USR workload (99.8% GET / 0.2% SET) over TCP; Rust spin-server with constant/exponential/bimodal service times (10 us mean); gdnsd 2.4.0 DNS over UDP. Each runs alongside PARSEC swaptions batch work, with 1,200 persistent connections from 6 client machines and all systems limited to 16 hyperthreads. Also load-burst tests (100k to 5M requests/s) and thread-operation microbenchmarks vs pthreads, Go and Arachne. Core reallocation every 5 us.
claimed_speedup: NSDI'19 paper: memcached (USR workload): Shenango handles over 5 million requests/s with 37 us median and 93 us 99.9th-percentile latency, keeping 99.9th-percentile latency below 100 us at 'one million more than ZygOS' (ZygOS keeps similar response times only up to ~4 million requests/s). Linux memcached reaches about 800,000 requests/s before 99th-percentile latency spikes (no batch work). With batch work, Linux's 99.9th-percentile latency at 0.4M requests/s goes from 83 us to over 2 ms. gdnsd DNS over UDP: Linux up to 900,000 requests/s (41 us median) vs Shenango 5.7 million requests/s, 'a 6.33x improvement' (36 us median, 73 us 99.9th percentile). Thread microbenchmarks (Table 2): spawn-join 148 ns vs 12,996 ns with Linux pthreads; condvar ping-pong 100 ns vs 1,900 ns. Per the abstract, unlike ZygOS, Shenango can linearly trade latency-sensitive throughput for batch-processing throughput.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. Repo Makefiles: gcc (runtime/IOKernel) and g++ (apps/bench) with -O3 -DNDEBUG -mssse3 (non-DEBUG build); Rust apps built with cargo --release on nightly. No compiler versions given.
hardware: Dual-socket server with 12-core Intel Xeon E5-2650v4 @ 2.20 GHz (first socket only, hyper-threads on, TurboBoost, C-states and frequency scaling disabled), 64 GB RAM, 10 Gb/s Intel 82599ES NIC; Ubuntu 18.04, kernel 4.15.0 (ZygOS on Ubuntu 16.04, kernel 4.11.0); load from six quad-core machines through a Mellanox SX1024 switch with ConnectX-3 Pro NICs
tradeoffs: Requires DPDK and a dedicated IOKernel scheduling process; kernel-bypass core reallocation adds operational complexity
caveats: The README says 'This repository is no longer maintained' and points to the successor shenango/caladan. The last commit (2024-11-05) only adds that README notice, so the entry stays marked abandoned. By commit age alone (about 23 months) the rule would give 'stale'. The benchmark_url abstract page has only the qualitative claim; the numbers are in the paper PDF. ZygOS reaches higher peak memcached throughput than Shenango, but at a high latency cost. At memcached's very short service times (<2 us) the IOKernel becomes the bottleneck. Shenango dedicates a full core (2 hyperthreads) to the IOKernel. The main win is CPU efficiency (batch throughput recovered) at equal tail latency, not raw speed over kernel-bypass stacks. The successor Caladan (shenango/caladan, Apache-2.0, 200 stars, pushed 2026-09-25) was published at OSDI'20, not NSDI'20: https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi20/presentation/fried. Its abstract claims an 11,000x tail-latency reduction vs Parties (580 ms to 52 us).
found_via: arXiv query 'Shenango scheduling microsecond' -> https://www.usenix.org/conference/nsdi19/presentation/ousterhout

verification.tier_reason: The peer-reviewed NSDI'19 paper (PDF linked from the benchmark_url page) reports numeric wins against Linux and ZygOS on stated hardware (Xeon E5-2650v4, Intel 82599ES). The repo has benchmark code (apps/synthetic with linux-server/linux-client modes, apps/bench with gcc/g++ -O3 Makefiles), but the paper states no compiler versions or flags, and none for the baseline builds (memcached 1.5.6, gdnsd 2.4.0, ZygOS/Linux spin-servers from the ZygOS repo), so it is not A.
verification.notes: Tier B confirmed, and numbers are now filled in from the paper PDF. The strongest baseline number is 6.33x DNS throughput vs Linux gdnsd. The abandoned tag is kept because the maintainers' README declares it unmaintained; by the commit-age rule alone it would be 'stale', so the orchestrator may want to decide. Caladan (OSDI'20, with numbers) may deserve its own entry; the searcher's 404 came from using the wrong venue (NSDI'20).

No single numeric multiplier is stated on that page.

corrected_fields.caveats: The repository's own README states 'This repository is no longer maintained' and directs users to the successor shenango/caladan; marked abandoned here despite a 2024 push because the maintainers themselves declared it superseded. No exact numeric multiplier for the ZygOS/Linux comparison was found on the pages opened this session, only the qualitative claim quoted above. The successor, shenango/caladan (200 stars, Apache-2.0, actively pushed as of 2026-09-25), was checked but its NSDI'20 paper page 404'd and its README states no quantified comparison, so Caladan itself is not reported here as a separate entry.

name: aeronet
workload: wrk-driven HTTP/1.1 benchmark (1 thread, 30s duration, 5s warmup) across headers/body/body-codec/static/cpu/mixed/files/routing scenarios at 10 and 100 connections, run in CI against scripted competitor servers built from the same harness.
claimed_speedup: vs beast (10 conns): headers 12,035.73 vs 4,376.77 req/s (2.75x), static 54,259.34 vs 49,281.00 (1.10x), routing 57,644.49 vs 47,995.38 (1.20x). vs go net/http (10 conns): headers 12,035.73 vs 3,996.83 (3.0x), static 54,259.34 vs 25,399.27 (2.14x), routing 57,644.49 vs 28,141.20 (2.05x), mixed 25,261.40 vs 9,003.95 (2.81x), body 3,827.02 vs 407.32 (9.4x); at 100 conns aeronet leads go net/http in every scenario (e.g. static 93,479.14 vs 37,787.70, routing 91,957.05 vs 44,446.00) (all derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: CMake Release (-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release, Ninja) on GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest with apt build-essential GCC (workflow comment: 'Both use GCC'); GCC version not pinned; no explicit -O flags beyond the CMake Release default; Go server built with stdlib net/http; Beast server built in the same Release CMake config
tradeoffs: Linux-focused for peak performance (also supports macOS/Windows); benchmark harness builds and runs competitor servers (drogon, pistache, crow, beast, Rust Axum, Java Undertow, Go net/http, Python) itself in CI rather than using each project's own tuned deployment configuration, so absolute numbers may not reflect each competitor's best-case tuning.
caveats: First-party CI benchmark (project builds and runs all competitors itself); GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner is a generic shared/virtualized host with no CPU model stated, and the GCC version is not pinned, so this falls short of Tier A despite public benchmark code and full wrk parameters. Dashboard is regenerated on every push to main (30s x1 sample) and weekly (45s x3-sample median), so numbers move run-to-run. aeronet does not beat Boost.Beast everywhere: in the 2026-09-26 run Beast was faster on cpu at 10 conns (7,354.19 vs 7,120.30), static at 100 conns (96,444.03 vs 93,479.14) and routing at 100 conns (100,848.37 vs 91,957.05); drogon also beat aeronet on static at 100 conns (99,662.33) and files at 100 conns (2,496.81 vs 2,490.52). aeronet beat Go net/http in all 16 scenario/connection cells. LICENSE is MIT text with an unfilled '[year] [fullname]' placeholder (GitHub reports NOASSERTION).

name: Demikernel
workload: SOSP'21: 64 B echo server/client (1M echos, 5 runs); UDP relay (TURN) server driven by a Linux traffic generator; Redis via redis-benchmark GET/SET (64 B values, 1M keys, in-memory and with a per-SET fsync append-only log); TxnStore under YCSB-t. Compared against Linux POSIX sockets/epoll, io_uring and kernel-bypass systems (eRPC, Shenango, Caladan, DPDK testpmd, RDMA perftest). The 2019 blog ran the Redis benchmark on CloudLab.
claimed_speedup: SOSP'21 paper, 64 B echo RTT on Linux hosts (Fig. 5): Linux POSIX 30.4 us vs Catnip (DPDK) UDP 6.0 us + 0.025 us of Demikernel time, Catnip TCP 7.1 + 0.053 us, Catmint (RDMA) 5.3 + 0.949 us. That is about 4.3-5x lower RTT with Catnip (derived from page data). UDP relay server (Fig. 10): average 24.9 us on Linux vs 13.9 us on Catnip, p99 27.6 vs 14.9 us; the paper says 'Catnip reduces the server-side latency per request by 11us on average and 13.7us at the p99' (io_uring: 24.4/25.8 us). Redis in-memory peak throughput vs unmodified Redis on Linux (Fig. 11): 'Catmint gives 2x throughput, and Catnip offers 20% better throughput'. Azure VM: 'Catnip offers a 5x latency improvement over the Linux kernel'. The 2019 first-party blog (CloudLab Redis) says '60% of the latency comes from the OS kernel and its interface' (30% from interface inefficiency, another 30% removed by RDMA/DPDK kernel bypass).
hardware: SOSP'21 Linux cluster: 5 servers with 20-core dual-socket Intel Xeon Silver 4114 @ 2.2 GHz, Mellanox CX-5 100 Gbps NICs, Arista 7060CX 100 Gbps switch, Intel Optane 800P NVMe. Windows cluster: 14-core dual-socket Xeon 2690 @ 2.6 GHz with Mellanox CX-4 56 Gbps. The 2019 blog used CloudLab with a 25Gb network and Mellanox CX-4 NICs.
tradeoffs: Project explicitly labeled a research prototype with 'no guarantees'; requires DPDK/RDMA hardware for the kernel-bypass LibOSes (catnip); Linux-socket LibOS (catnap) has no bypass benefit by itself
caveats: The SOSP'21 paper is open access at the first author's site; the ACM DL PDF returned HTTP 403 to automated fetches, but the paper is not paywalled. The wins are against the Linux kernel sockets/epoll path. Against other kernel-bypass stacks Demikernel is competitive rather than uniformly faster: Catnip echo is 1.7 us slower than Caladan, Catnip (UDP) reaches 70% of Caladan's peak throughput, and Catmint reaches 46% of eRPC's. The Linux-sockets LibOS (Catnap) busy-polls a full core and has lower Redis peak throughput than unmodified Redis. The gains need DPDK/RDMA-capable NICs, and the README calls the project a prototype with no guarantees. The paper states no Rust/compiler version or build flags.

claimed_speedup: 40-54% more requests/sec than tuned nginx at the same connection counts (64 conns: 358,428 vs 256,046 req/s = +40%; 1024 conns: 315,095 vs 204,644 = +54%; 4096 conns: 276,195 vs 184,395 = +50%); 28-34% less CPU per request (5.8-7.5us vs nginx's 8.1-11.1us); half the instructions per request (17,583 vs 35,831) (verbatim from README table)

name: ChaChaCha
baseline: OpenSSL ChaCha20/ChaCha20-Poly1305 (assembly and EVP), BoringSSL stitched AVX2 ChaCha20-Poly1305
workload: ChaCha20 and ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD seal/open at protocol-realistic sizes (QUIC 1200-1350B, WireGuard 1360-1420B, 4KB TLS record, 9000B jumbo, 16384B TLS 1.3 max record, 32-64KiB bulk) measured in core cycles/byte via perf_event_open, pinned to one core, best-of-7 internal reps x best-of-3 runs, on AMD EPYC 9655 (Zen 5) and AMD EPYC 4244P (Zen 4)
claimed_speedup: Page percentages are cycles/byte reductions, (theirs - ours)/theirs, not throughput ratios. Zen 5 AEAD real-world bands vs OpenSSL (vendored asm, called without EVP): seal +19.3% to +45.4% (WireGuard 1360-1420B +45.4%, i.e. 1.83x throughput derived from page data; 16384B +22.4%); open +20.9% to +47.6%. Zen 5 vs BoringSSL stitched AVX2: seal +49.4% to +57.1%, open +53.5% to +57.4%. Zen 5 vs Intel IPsec-MB (best of its two entry points): seal +3.8% to +16.8%, open +4.7% to +19.9%. Zen 4 AEAD vs OpenSSL: seal +8.9% to +33.0%, open +9.2% to +32.5%; vs BoringSSL +30.8% to +37.5%; vs Intel -1.3% to +8.9% (loses at Jumbo 8900-9000B). Raw AVX-512 ChaCha20: +25.0% to +33.1% vs the best other implementation (Intel) on Zen 5 for bands of 4KB and above (vs OpenSSL 16x about +29% to +35%, derived from page data); Zen 4 +5.0% to +7.6% vs best other (vs OpenSSL about +8% to +15%, derived from page data); ours loses to Intel at QUIC/WireGuard sizes (-7.5%/-3.9% Zen 5, -26.0%/-16.5% Zen 4). Raw AVX2 ChaCha20 vs best other (OpenSSL/BoringSSL): +10.0% to +10.8% on Zen 5 and +5.4% to +8.1% on Zen 4 for bands of 4KB and above; about 0% at 1200-1420B.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (version not stated; README requires Linux x86-64 with gcc and make), Makefile CFLAGS ?= -O2 -Wall for C harness/glue, ASFLAGS=-Wa,--noexecstack; kernels are perlasm-generated assembly assembled by gcc plus NASM (-f elf64) for poly1305_ifma.asm and the Intel vendor kernels
hardware: AMD EPYC 9655 (Zen 5, Turin) and AMD EPYC 4244P (Zen 4)
tradeoffs: x86-64 AVX2/AVX-512 only (no portable/scalar-only fallback path shown as competitive); OpenSSL is measured both as raw vendored assembly (openssl-asm) and via EVP (openssl-evp) which carries provider dispatch overhead, so the EVP-vs-EVP comparison would show an even larger margin than the asm-vs-asm numbers quoted; BoringSSL comparison for AVX-512 is AEAD-only since BoringSSL has no AVX-512 ChaCha20 raw kernel; single author, very new/unreviewed project
caveats: Single-author project with 1 GitHub star and no independent reproduction. Only two AMD CPUs tested (Zen 5 EPYC 9655, Zen 4 EPYC 4244P); no Intel CPU results. The AEAD 'OpenSSL' column is OpenSSL's vendored assembly called directly (no stitched AEAD in OpenSSL); OpenSSL EVP has higher fixed per-call cost (1419/1773 cycles vs 650/550 for asm). Ours is slower than OpenSSL asm on small messages (Zen 5 seal 64-256B: -19.6% to -24.0%; Zen 4 seal 64-256B: -9.5% to -23.4%) and roughly equal at exactly 1024B. Page flags power-of-two lengths (1024/2048/4096...) as flattering batch boundaries and uses realistic protocol-size bands for headline tables. Page GB/s figures assume a nominal 3.0 GHz; c/B is the real metric. Methodology is careful: perf_event_open core cycles, pinned core, alternating order, best of 7 x best of 3, round-trip correctness check before timing.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code 'handshakes per second' "faster" (surfaced via a broader ChaCha20 AVX-512/TLS-record code search, then opened repo README and result.md directly)

The gcc version is not stated, but the timed kernels are hand-written perlasm/NASM assembly.

License Apache-2.0, 1 star, last commit 2026-09-21, not fork, not archived: metadata confirmed.

name: curve25519 (mehdi sotoodeh / "Mehdi")
baseline: OpenSSL 1.1.1 EVP_PKEY API: EVP_PKEY_ED25519 (CreateKeyPair, SignMessage via EVP_DigestSign) and EVP_PKEY_X25519 (CalculatePublicKey, CreateSharedKey via EVP_PKEY_derive)
workload: test/openssl_test.c: Ed25519 key-pair creation, X25519 public-key derivation, X25519 shared-secret computation and Ed25519 signing of a 32-byte message; min of 100 runs per operation timed with rdtsc (TSC ticks, minus rdtsc overhead), comparing the x86-64 assembly library build ('make asm && make openssl') against OpenSSL's EVP_PKEY API; outputs are memcmp-checked for equality
claimed_speedup: README OpenSSL comparison (HP EliteBook 755 G5, Ubuntu 18.04.2, OpenSSL 1.1.1; TSC cycles, the '@3.4GHz' usec figures are a fixed constant in the test code): CreateKeyPair 74,822 vs 210,738 cycles (ratio 2.817, delta 64.50%); CalculatePublicKey 316,096 vs 208,714 (ratio 0.660, Mehdi 51.45% slower); CreateSharedKey 270,930 vs 442,750 (ratio 1.634, delta 38.81%); SignMessage 78,628 vs 425,656 (ratio 5.414, delta 81.53%). The OpenSSL timed region also includes EVP_PKEY creation from the raw secret (plus peer-key and context setup for CreateSharedKey), while the Mehdi SignMessage call receives a precomputed 64-byte private+public key, so the CreateSharedKey and SignMessage margins are not like-for-like. Separately, X25519 base-point multiplication is 5.33x to 19.59x faster than curve25519-donna across the README platform/compiler table (README text says 6.2 to 19.5); fastest 43,229 cycles (W7-64/MASM V1.1, Intel Core i7-2670QM).
compiler_and_flags: gcc via Rules.mk (version not stated for the OpenSSL run); source/asm64/Makefile compiles the C glue with -O2 -m64 -Wall -Wno-format -DUSE_ASM_LIB and assembles amd64.gnu/*.s with 'as --64'; test objects, including openssl_test.c, use -O2; RELEASE=1 adds -DNDEBUG, otherwise -g -D_DEBUG. The portable-C library (source/Makefile) also uses -O2. Donna table: VS2010/MASM, GNU assembler 2.25 (mingw) and gcc 4.5.3 (Cygwin-32).
hardware: OpenSSL comparison: HP EliteBook 755 G5 laptop, x86_64 (CPU model not stated), Ubuntu 18.04.2; donna comparison and internal cycle tables: Intel Core i7-2670QM
tradeoffs: One of four benchmarked operations (CalculatePublicKey) is markedly slower than OpenSSL, so the library is not a strict win across the board; portable-C build has no stated optimization level (only the asm build is used for the OpenSSL comparison); constant-time/blinding variants are slower than the non-hardened V1.1 numbers; abandoned since 2020, predates OpenSSL 3.x and modern OpenSSL X25519/Ed25519 assembly optimizations, so the OpenSSL side of the comparison is likely stale
caveats: OpenSSL comparison dates from June 2019 (commit 'Performance comparison with OpenSSL') against OpenSSL 1.1.1 on one laptop whose CPU model is not given. OpenSSL-side timings include EVP_PKEY object creation from the raw secret inside the timed loop, and the Mehdi SignMessage side gets a precomputed public key, so the SignMessage and CreateSharedKey margins are inflated; the like-for-like CalculatePublicKey (X25519) row shows this library 51.45% slower than OpenSSL. Minimum of 100 TSC-timed runs, not core cycles. Current OpenSSL 3.x results are unknown. The curve25519-donna comparison (5.33x-19.59x) uses a different, non-list baseline across different compilers/platforms. Repo has had no commits since 2020-04-20.

name: EverCrypt (HACL*) Curve25519 (Vale-optimized)
workload: Curve25519 scalar multiplication (the X25519 ECDH used in TLS 1.3), average CPU cycles per operation. The other implementations were measured in-kernel with Donenfeld's kbench9000 cycle counter. OpenSSL was measured 'using the same script, but in user space', because it cannot be called from the kernel.
claimed_speedup: EverCrypt's targeted Curve25519 (Low* C plus Vale Intel ADX asm) takes 113,614 CPU cycles per scalar multiplication. OpenSSL's ADX asm takes 118,604. That is about 4.2% fewer cycles, or about 1.04x (derived from page data, Figure 9 of 'EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider', IEEE S&P 2020). The paper's text says EverCrypt beats Oliveira et al. (115,122 cycles) by about 1%, and that Oliveira et al. 'in turn exceeds that of OpenSSL by 3%'. It also says EverCrypt beats Erbsen et al./fiat-crypto (145,248 cycles) by 22%.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 7.3, -O3 -march=native -mtune=native
hardware: Intel Kaby Lake i7-7560 (the paper's wording; the record's i7-7560U suffix is not in the paper)
stars_or_usage: 1,837 stars. hacl-star.github.io says code from HACL*, ValeCrypt and EverCrypt is deployed in Mozilla Firefox's NSS, the Linux kernel, mbedTLS, the Tezos blockchain, the ElectionGuard SDK and the WireGuard VPN.
tradeoffs: Source is written in F*/Low*/Vale and compiled via KaRaMeL to C/assembly rather than hand-written C; gains formal proofs of memory safety, functional correctness and secret-independence (constant-time) at the cost of a heavy build toolchain (F*, KaRaMeL, Vale) compared to a plain C/asm library.
caveats: The gain over OpenSSL is only about 4% in cycles (derived). The record's '~3% over OpenSSL' misreads the paper: that 3% is Oliveira et al. over OpenSSL. The result is from one 2017-era Kaby Lake CPU, against an OpenSSL build from 2018-19 (commit e8fb288). OpenSSL ran in user space while the other implementations ran in-kernel via kbench9000, so the environments differ. The public kbench9000 kb/x25519 branch holds the EverCrypt/Vale code and the other contenders but no OpenSSL harness, so the OpenSSL comparison cannot be fully reproduced from public code. The paper's AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 figures (Figures 7-8, i9-9900K) say only that EverCrypt 'meets or exceeds' OpenSSL, so do not extrapolate to other primitives. The README calls hacl-star the research home and points production users to https://github.com/cryspen/hacl-packages. The repo is Apache-2.0, and the generated C code is also MIT.
found_via: Google Scholar / arXiv / ACM DL / IEEE: HACL* GitHub README citation trail to the EverCrypt IEEE S&P'20 paper PDF (project-everest.github.io/assets/evercrypt.pdf), located after arXiv queries for 'verified cryptographic OpenSSL performance' surfaced only related/adjacent papers

Downgraded A to B because the public benchmark harness has no OpenSSL. Metadata checked with gh: Apache-2.0, not a fork, not archived, 1,837 stars, last commit 2026-04-10, so 'active' holds.

name: ztls
workload: Sans-I/O TLS 1.3 in-memory application-data round trips (client-to-server, server-to-client, ping-pong) at record sizes 16B, 128B, 1350B, 8192B, 16384B, across TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384, and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256, over caller-owned in-memory transport (no sockets), n=10 captures with formal confidence intervals
claimed_speedup: Headline row (AppPingPong AES-128-GCM 1350B, x86_64 c7i.2xlarge, n=10): ztls 790.7 ns/op vs rustls 1447.5 ns/op (1.83x) vs OpenSSL libssl 1820.5 ns/op (2.30x). ztls executes 42.7% of libssl's cycles/op and 54.8% of rustls's on that row (row-perf capture). Faster than libssl on all 45 comparable app-data rows on x86_64, aarch64 and macOS (from +4% on ChaCha20 16384B ping-pong on aarch64 to +261% on AES-128-GCM 16B client-to-server on x86_64). Faster than rustls on all 30 AES-GCM rows per platform (x86_64 +65% to +131%). On x86_64 it loses to rustls on ChaCha20-Poly1305 at 16B/128B (-50% to -56%) and, per the benchstat file, by about 6% at 1350B (the page calls this an approximate tie).
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.15.2, -Doptimize=ReleaseFast, native CPU target, crypto_backend=openssl (OpenSSL 3.6.3 libcrypto via nix); comparison backends OpenSSL 3.6.3 libssl and rustls 0.23.40 (x86_64) / 0.23.41 (aarch64, macOS) release profile, rustc 1.97.0 on the x86_64 capture; benchstat over --count 10 --benchtime 500ms. Captured at git revisions 2c102a5 (x86_64), e39f5a6 (aarch64) and 80083f5 (macOS), before ztls required Zig 0.16
hardware: AWS c7i.2xlarge (Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, x86_64, KVM guest); AWS c7g.2xlarge, which the page and README call Graviton4 but whose committed lscpu metadata shows Neoverse-V1 / 'AWS Graviton3 CPU @ 2.6GHz'; Apple M1 Max (macOS Darwin 24.6)
tradeoffs: Pre-alpha, API not stable; TLS 1.3 only (no 1.2 fallback, no DTLS, no Windows); crypto primitives (AEAD, ECDHE, signatures, SHA-2) are still delegated to a libcrypto backend (OpenSSL, AWS-LC, or BoringSSL) which allocates during setup, so the zero-allocation claim covers only ztls's own framing/parsing/transcript code, not the crypto backend; loses to rustls on small ChaCha20-Poly1305 records on x86_64; full-handshake row is explicitly documented as non-equivalent across implementations (different certificate-verification scope) and the project itself says not to quote it as a comparison
caveats: Pre-alpha single-author project (7 stars) with no independent reproduction. ztls delegates AEAD, key exchange and SHA-2 to a libcrypto backend (OpenSSL 3.6.3 in all headline captures), the same library as the libssl baseline, so the win over libssl is TLS record-layer and wrapper overhead (WPACKET, tls13_cipher, BIO copies), not faster crypto. Only application-data rows over in-memory transport are compared; the handshake row is explicitly non-equivalent and not claimed. libssl gets one warm-up round while ztls and rustls do not. The captures used Zig 0.15.2 at older revisions, and current ztls requires Zig 0.16. The page labels the c7g.2xlarge host Graviton4, but its lscpu metadata says Graviton3 (Neoverse-V1).

name: AWS-LC
workload: HAProxy 3.1-dev1 (2024-06-26) server-only full TLS handshake (RSA, one HTTP request per new connection, no resumption) and end-to-end TLS session resumption from tickets on both the client and backend sides (10 daisy-chained proxy instances), connections/sec vs thread count up to 64, with pthread rwlocks and with HAProxy's lightweight locks (USE_PTHREAD_EMULATION); the TLS protocol version is not stated
claimed_speedup: HAProxy 3.1-dev1 on a 64-core Graviton4, at 64 threads (bar charts on page). Full TLS handshake (RSA, new conn/s): AWS-LC v1.32.0+30 commits 63.1k (same with or without the C11 build) vs OpenSSL 1.1.1w 48.3k, OpenSSL 3.1.6-3.4.0-dev 42.6-43.2k, OpenSSL 3.0.2/3.0.14 21.2-21.3k (~1.31x vs 1.1.1w, ~1.46-1.48x vs 3.1+, ~3.0x vs 3.0.x; derived from page data). The older AWS-LC 1.29.0 reached only 45.2k (45.7k with -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11), below OpenSSL 1.1.1w, because of a CPU-detection bug. TLS resumption (end-to-end conn/s): AWS-LC 1.29.0 built with -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 186.3k (text: ~183k; v1.32+30-c11 183.7k) with either lock type, vs OpenSSL 1.1.1w 17.8k (pthread locks) / 124.1k (HAProxy locks), OpenSSL 3.1-3.4-dev 23.1-27.9k, OpenSSL 3.0.14 3.7k / 8.1k, OpenSSL 3.0.2 1.6k / 2.3k. The page text says '~20% higher than WolfSSL and 50% higher than OpenSSL 1.1.1w'. The default C99 AWS-LC builds (1.29.0 and 1.32+30) collapsed to 8.4-8.5k with pthread locks and 38.4k with HAProxy locks.
compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.4 (stated on page); AWS-LC's CMake config forced C99 (pthread-rwlock refcounting) unless -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 was set; HAProxy built with and without USE_PTHREAD_EMULATION=1; optimization flags not stated
hardware: AWS r8g.16xlarge instance, 64 Graviton4 (ARM Neoverse V2) cores
license: Apache-2.0 OR ISC for new AWS-LC code; the LICENSE file lists BoringSSL-derived code as ISC/Apache-2.0, OpenSSL-derived code as Apache-2.0, and bundled parts as MIT, BSD-3-Clause and CC0 (GitHub reports NOASSERTION)
stars_or_usage: 835 stars; used internally at AWS (s2n-tls, AWS SDKs, AWS-LC-rs) for TLS/crypto
tradeoffs: Code inherited from BoringSSL/OpenSSL retains original ISC/OpenSSL-era licensing alongside AWS-LC's own Apache-2.0/ISC files (mixed licensing across the tree); default build configuration silently underperforms until C11 is forced
caveats: Independent third-party benchmark (HAProxy Technologies; tests mid-2024, published 2025-05-06), although AWS supplied HAProxy's AWS-LC patches. The ~63k full-handshake figure is for AWS-LC v1.32.0 plus 30 commits, not 1.29.0; 1.29.0 (~45k) trailed OpenSSL 1.1.1w in that test. Default builds at the time (C99, lock-based refcounting) collapsed in the resumption test to ~8.5k conn/s at 64 threads, worse than OpenSSL 1.1.1w and 3.1+ with pthread locks, until rebuilt with -DCMAKE_C_STANDARD=11 (the page says this was fixed upstream). Only one ARM platform (Graviton4) was tested; gcc 11.4 is stated but optimization flags and the test scripts are not published. Small CC0 parts carry no patent grant.

name: Graviola
workload: One process per run: decode 3 PEM files, then a full TLS 1.3 handshake over loopback TCP (server in main thread, client in another thread), then exit with no application data. wtx TLS stack with a swappable crypto backend (aws-lc-rs, Graviola, ring, OpenSSL via openssl-sys). 5 certificate signature algorithms x 3 key agreements (secp256r1, secp384r1, x25519) x 3 cipher suites. Timed with hyperfine -N, 10 runs after 10 warmups; mean plotted.
claimed_speedup: Page text: "OpenSSL is the slower library" and "Graviola is a promising new cryptography library". Numbers exist only as bar charts (hyperfine mean wall time per process, seconds, 0-0.010 s axis), not box plots. From the SVG bar heights (derived from page data): Graviola about 1.26-5.90 ms vs OpenSSL about 4.41-10.20 ms per full handshake process, about 1.6-3.8x; OpenSSL is slowest in all 45 combinations; Graviola is fastest in only 16 of 45 (ring or aws-lc-rs tie or win the rest).
compiler_and_flags: rustc version not stated (bench Cargo.toml: edition 2024, rust-version = 1.96, wtx 0.49 with 'nightly' feature); cargo profile 'deploy': opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1, panic=abort, debug-assertions and overflow-checks off (from wtx-bench.tar.xz). OpenSSL version and build flags not stated.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core, 32GB DDR4, Corsair Force MP510 SSD, Linux Fedora kernel 7.0.11-200.fc44.x86_64
tradeoffs: Rust only; requires aarch64 with NEON+PMULL or x86_64 with AVX2/ADX/BMI2/PCLMULQDQ (excludes older CPUs like Raspberry Pi 4); very new/unaudited; RSA key generation is not side-channel-safe; built primarily as a rustls CryptoProvider rather than a standalone TLS stack
caveats: Independent third-party blog by the wtx author, not a well-known suite; code is public in wtx-bench.tar.xz but rustc and OpenSSL versions are not stated. Graviola is fastest in only 16 of 45 combinations; ring matches or beats it on several, and aws-lc-rs beats it with ECDSA-P384 certificates. Numbers exist only in SVG bar charts (means of 10 runs). Graviola's own jbp.io/graviola page (Ryzen 9 7940HS, Apple M2, no compiler/flags) compares only against ring, aws-lc-rs, rustcrypto, golang, dalek and libcrux, not OpenSSL. name: picotls "fusion" AES-GCM engine
workload: AES-GCM AEAD encryption throughput (bytes/s) for QUIC-sized 1440-byte blocks and 16KB blocks, with 13-byte AAD. fusionbench.c uses a 16-byte key, so this is AES-128-GCM; the chart does not label the key size, and AES-256 support was still a to-do in the PR. The chart also shows fusion with QUIC header protection computed in parallel.
claimed_speedup: At 1440-byte AEAD blocks, fusion's throughput is 5.86e9 vs 4.43e9 B/s on Core i5 9400 (1.32x), 4.91e9 vs 3.61e9 on Ryzen 3 3200G (1.36x) and 3.07e9 vs 2.32e9 on Core m3 6Y30 (1.32x). The baseline is OpenSSL 1.1.1g in full-AEAD mode (derived from page data). At 16384-byte blocks the gap shrinks to 1.01-1.15x. The PR text itself says OpenSSL loses ~30% throughput at 1440 bytes compared with 16KB, while fusion cuts that overhead to ~10%. Against OpenSSL's AES-GCM-core-only numbers (no AAD, IV setup or finalization), fusion at 1440 bytes is 1.03-1.14x.
hardware: Intel Core i5 9400 @4GHz, AMD Ryzen 3 3200G @3.6GHz, Intel Core m3 6Y30 @2.2GHz (chart labels in the PR)
stars_or_usage: 641 stars; used in the H2O HTTP server
tradeoffs: Fusion is x86-64-specific and written in plain C (not hand assembly) to keep pipelines full for short AEAD blocks; it's one of four interchangeable crypto backends in picotls (OpenSSL, minicrypto, fusion, libaegis), so using it is opt-in and the OpenSSL backend remains the default for portability.
caveats: The PR states no compiler or flags, and the chart gives no cycles/byte. The CPU models are on the chart, contrary to the original record. The baseline is OpenSSL 1.1.1g from 2020, now several major releases old, and OpenSSL was measured with `openssl speed -aead` rather than the same harness as fusion. The win is mainly at short (QUIC-sized) blocks, 1.3x or more; at 16KB it is 1-15%. Fusion is x86-64 only and needs AES-NI, PCLMUL and AVX2. The repo has no top-level LICENSE file. The README says MIT, and lib/fusion.c is under both Apache-2.0 and MIT because its transformH function is derived from OpenSSL. The minicrypto binding pulls in cifra (CC0; no patent grant) and micro-ecc (BSD-2-Clause). The repo's t/ptlsbench.c now benchmarks fusion and OpenSSL AEADs side by side, but no published results with methodology were found.

name: Tempesta FW (Tempesta TLS)
workload: Server-side full and abbreviated TLS 1.2 handshakes (ECDHE+ECDSA over NIST P-256) measured with the project's own tls-perf tool and wrk, comparing Nginx 1.19.1/OpenSSL 1.1.1d against Tempesta FW's in-Linux-kernel TLS handshake implementation, on a 1-vCPU KVM VM and on 2-node bare-metal servers
claimed_speedup: 40-80% more TLS connections/sec than Nginx/OpenSSL and up to 4x lower latency in some tests; concretely: 1-CPU VM new-session RPS 2,180 vs 1,545 (+41%), avg latency 307ms vs 1,340ms (-77%); 2-CPU bare-metal session-resumption 35,263 vs 19,203 conn/s (+83%); 2-CPU bare-metal new-session RPS only 7,921 vs 7,426 (+6%). Raw crypto op/s were slower than OpenSSL: ECDSA 27,261 vs OpenSSL's 36,472 op/s, ECDHE 6,690 vs OpenSSL's 16,619 op/s -- the throughput win comes from avoiding user/kernel context switches and heap allocation, not from faster math.
hardware: 1 vCPU KVM VM on Intel Core i7-6500U host (no vAPIC), virtio_net; 2-node bare-metal cluster with Intel Xeon E3-1240v5 CPUs and Mellanox ConnectX-2 10GbE, Linux kernel 5.7 (also compared to 4.14)
tradeoffs: Linux-kernel-only (x86-64 with AVX/BMI/ADX required, no generic C fallback for the crypto routines), puts TLS handshake code in kernel space (larger attack surface / TCB), GPLv2 licensing, and the paper itself reports tail-latency spikes up to 30x worse in the worst case on bare metal under SoftIRQ load
caveats: This is a first-party paper/benchmark by the Tempesta Technologies team (NetDev 0x14 conference paper, July 2020), not independent peer review, so it is capped at tier C despite the public benchmark tool (tls-perf) and stated hardware; compiler and build flags are not given. The headline 40-80% figure applies mainly to the 1-vCPU VM and to session resumption; the bare-metal new-session gain was only +6%. On bare metal Nginx/OpenSSL had lower average and 95th-percentile latency (the paper says 50-170% lower for new sessions and 4-9% for resumption), and Tempesta showed large tail-latency spikes (max latency up to +3000%, 28,262 vs 925 ms on resumption). The raw ECDSA/ECDHE op/s were lower than OpenSSL even though Tempesta's figures include ephemeral key generation, so that comparison is not like-for-like. Only x86-64 with AVX/BMI/ADX is supported, and the design relies on RDRAND randomization, which SRBDS microcode mitigations slow. Test hardware and kernel (5.7, 2020) are dated, and the code has changed since.

name: Homa (HomaModule) — Linux kernel implementation of the Homa RPC transport protocol
workload: 40-node CloudLab cluster; basic back-to-back single-client RPC latency/throughput (Table 2) plus four of the 'Montazeri' request/response workloads under high network load, measuring P50/P99/P999 tail latency across message sizes; Homa is explicitly designed as a transport for datacenter RPC frameworks (paper names gRPC and Apache Thrift as the frameworks it targets)
claimed_speedup: 40-node cluster benchmark at high load (workloads W2-W5): for short messages, P99 latency is 19-72x lower than TCP and 7-83x lower than DCTCP (the abstract summarises this as 7-83x lower than TCP and DCTCP). For short messages, P50 is 3.5-7.5x lower than TCP and 2.7-3.8x lower than DCTCP. Homa's P50 and P99 are lower than TCP/DCTCP at every message size, but the 7-83x range applies only to short messages. Best-case 100-byte RTT: 15.1us (Homa) vs 23.4us (TCP) vs 24.1us (DCTCP). Client and server RPC rate: 1.6 vs 1.0 Mops/sec (60% higher).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The kernel module is built with kbuild against Linux 5.4.80 using the kernel's own flags. The repo's current util/Makefile builds the cp_node benchmark driver with g++ -Wall -Werror -fno-strict-aliasing -O3. No compiler version is given anywhere.
hardware: CloudLab xl170 nodes: Intel Xeon E5-2640v4 (10 cores, 2.4GHz), 4x16GB DDR4-2400, Intel DC S3520 480GB SSD, Mellanox ConnectX-4 25Gbps NIC, Mellanox 2410 switch, 40-node cluster
license: BSD-2-Clause OR GPL-2.0+ (per-file SPDX headers on the module and benchmark sources; a few test/tool files are BSD-1-Clause or GPL-2.0; no top-level LICENSE file)
tradeoffs: Requires a custom Linux kernel module (no macOS/Windows, no unprivileged/userspace-only path); new homa_send/homa_recv/homa_reply socket API is not backward-compatible with existing TCP/UDP socket code, so gRPC/Thrift apps need a shim (see grpc_homa) to use it transparently; needs specific NIC support (Mellanox ConnectX-4/5/6, Intel E810 verified); paper states small-message throughput is still 5-10x below raw NIC line rate due to software/kernel overhead.
caveats: The 7-83x win is for P99 latency of short messages under high load, not for raw bandwidth. The paper's own Table 2 shows single-connection 500KB throughput where Homa (10.0 Gbps) is LOWER than TCP (20.3 Gbps); multi-RPC throughput is equal (23.8 vs 23.9 Gbps). The baseline is Linux kernel TCP/DCTCP, not gRPC or Thrift themselves; the RPC-framework link goes through the separate, less mature PlatformLab/grpc_homa shim (reported as a companion entry). The paper's numbers come from the 2021 code on Linux 5.4.80. The module has since been heavily reworked (Homa 2.0, sendmsg/recvmsg API, Linux 6.17.8, upstreaming under way since Oct 2024), so current performance may differ. The license exists only in per-file SPDX headers (no LICENSE file).

name: wtx (gRPC server)
workload: Unary gRPC GetSum call (9-byte protobuf request) over plaintext HTTP/2 (h2c), h2load load generator with 256 and 1024 connections and 100 concurrent streams per connection, 5s duration, 3 runs with the best taken, on the HttpArena multi-language benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: 3.7-5.5x higher req/s than grpc-go: 3,990,708 vs 720,798 rps at 256 conns (avg latency 6.55ms vs 35.14ms); 3,620,970 vs 969,718 rps at 1024 conns (avg latency 26.89ms vs 88.65ms) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: wtx: Rust nightly-2026-06-27 (rust:1.95 base image), `RUSTFLAGS="-C target-cpu=native" cargo build --release` with release profile opt-level=3, lto="thin", codegen-units=1, panic="abort"; wtx 0.49 (features grpc-server, optimizations-std, quick-protobuf, tokio) per frameworks/wtx-grpc/Dockerfile and Cargo.toml in MDA2AV/HttpArena. grpc-go: Go 1.24 (golang:1.24-bookworm image), `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build`, google.golang.org/grpc v1.72.0, default grpc.NewServer() with GOMAXPROCS=NumCPU (frameworks/grpc-go).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 3995WX (Zen 2, 64 cores / 128 threads, single NUMA node, performance governor). Per HttpArena's Hardware & Topology docs, the server is pinned to a 64-thread cpuset (0-31,64-95 = 32 physical cores plus SMT siblings) and the load generator to the other half of the same chip; every run uses the same machine.
tradeoffs: wtx is a multi-protocol crate (gRPC, HTTP/2, WebSocket, Postgres, TLS, etc.) rather than a dedicated RPC-only library; requires nightly Rust; small community and, per its own README, 'not widely used and has not undergone security audits'; used noticeably more memory (727MiB-1022MiB) than grpc-go (310-922MiB) in this test.
caveats: wtx's server process used ~64 logical CPUs (6379-6383% cpu) versus grpc-go's ~44 (4339-4478% cpu) during the run, so throughput-per-core is not directly comparable, only end-to-end rps on shared hardware. The two results were not measured in the same session: grpc-go's unary-grpc numbers have been unchanged since an HttpArena results update on 2026-04-12 (commit f326f067), while wtx's current numbers come from a re-run on 2026-08-24 (PR #1300), and the harness evolved in between. wtx's earlier published unary-grpc numbers (2026-07-30 to 2026-08-24) were invalid: its handler returned an empty reply body that h2load did not detect; body validation caught it, the entry was disabled (PR #1291), fixed and re-validated in PR #1300. The figures above are the post-fix validated numbers. The harness (HttpArena, github.com/MDA2AV/HttpArena, MIT-licensed) is a general full-stack web-framework benchmark, not an RPC-specific shootout. The wtx-grpc entry was contributed by wtx's own author (c410-f3r, PRs #812 and #1056), so it is not a fully arms-length third party, although the Dockerfiles, build commands and raw JSON results are public and runs are done centrally by the HttpArena maintainers. grpc-go is labeled 'tuned' but runs a default grpc.NewServer(). tonic (Rust's main gRPC framework) has a directory in the repo and was benchmarked in an April 2026 pre-round (378,723 rps at 256 connections, commit 2b36f907), but it is absent from the current results, so no current same-language comparison exists. wtx is not the fastest entry on the board: zix, cardigan and swerver post about 6.8-7.0M rps in the same test.

name: SRPC (Sogou C++ Workflow RPC)
workload: Echo RPC with empty responses, driven by SRPC's own async client (benchmark/client.cc) against each server: same-machine QPS vs client threads (1-256, 1024B) and vs request size (16B-32KB, 100 threads); cross-machine QPS vs client threads (64-1024, 32B) and vs client processes (1-16 x 32 threads, 32B); latency CDFs at fixed QPS with 1% slow outliers (same-machine 10k QPS 1024B; cross-machine 32 clients x 2500 QPS 512B). Compared: SOGOU srpc-std, SOGOU brpc-std, SOGOU thrift-binary, BAIDU brpc-std and 'FACEBOOK thrift-binary' (Apache Thrift TNonblockingServer, TBinaryProtocol, 16 IO + 16 worker threads).
claimed_speedup: Read off README charts (derived from page data). Same machine, 1024B requests (benchmark3): SOGOU srpc-std ~310k QPS vs 'FACEBOOK thrift-binary' (Apache Thrift TNonblockingServer per benchmark/thrift_server.cc) ~145k at 32 client threads (~2.1x) and ~309k vs ~191k at 256 threads (~1.6x). Same machine, 100 threads, by request size (benchmark1): ~319k vs ~185k at 16B (~1.7x) to ~254k vs ~158k at 16KB (~1.6x) and ~205k vs ~133k at 32KB. Cross-machine: srpc ~470-520k vs ~167-220k at 64-1024 threads (benchmark2, ~2.3-2.8x); ~310k-670k vs ~145k-222k at 1-16 client processes (benchmark4, ~2.1-3.0x). Latency CDFs at fixed QPS (benchmark5/6): srpc stays under ~170us to the 99.9th percentile same-machine while Apache Thrift sits at ~235-480us; cross-machine Thrift is ~3.8ms+ at p80. SRPC's own thrift-binary server beats Apache Thrift by a little more (~331k vs ~145k at 32 threads). Versus Baidu brpc, srpc-std is slightly slower same-machine (~310k vs ~346k at 32 threads) but faster cross-machine (~520k vs ~405k; ~670k vs ~407k).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README. benchmark/CMakeLists.txt (2020 initial commit) builds SRPC's benchmark as CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE RelWithDebInfo with -Wall -fPIC -pipe -std=c++11 -fno-exceptions (now -std=c++17). A comment in benchmark/GNUmakefile builds the Thrift server with 'g++ ... -O2 -g -std=c++11'. No compiler version is given.
hardware: 2-chip/8-core/32-thread Intel Xeon E5-2630 v3 @2.40GHz, 128GB RAM, 10 Gigabit Ethernet
tradeoffs: Numbers read off line charts (no numeric table provided), so precision is approximate; tightly coupled to the Sogou C++ Workflow async engine, adding a dependency/learning curve beyond a plain RPC library.
caveats: Project's own benchmark. Values are read visually off PNG charts, not a numeric table. The chart label 'FACEBOOK thrift-binary' is the Apache Thrift C++ TNonblockingServer (benchmark/thrift_server.cc uses apache::thrift, TBinaryProtocol, 16 IO + 16 worker threads), not fbthrift. name: rest_rpc
baseline: brpc (Apache bRPC); gRPC only transitively, via brpc's own benchmark page
workload: Echo RPC with client and server on one bare-metal machine. The client loops sending 1K/8K/16K/64K strings of 'A', and the server echoes them back with no processing. Server threads equal CPU cores; clients ran single-threaded and with 6/10/20 threads. QPS is the average of several runs. This tested the 2019 C++11 rest_rpc (now the cpp11 branch), not the current C++20 master.
claimed_speedup: Higher QPS than brpc on a same-machine echo test. Single-thread client: 52631 vs 41667 QPS at 1K (~1.26x), ~1.24x at 8K, ~1.26x at 16K, 16949 vs 8982 at 64K (~1.89x). Multi-thread 1K: 200000 vs 103448 at 6 threads (~1.93x), ~1.50x at 10, ~1.19x at 20. Multi-thread 64K: ~1.72x/1.92x/1.69x at 6/10/20 threads (ratios derived from page data). The page says rest_rpc is almost 2x brpc at 64K. The README's 'far exceeds gRPC' is not measured anywhere; it rests on brpc's own benchmark ranking gRPC last.
compiler_and_flags: g++ (Ubuntu 8.2.0-1ubuntu2~18.04) 8.2.0; both projects built with cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (explicit flags not listed)
hardware: Intel Core i5-9400F @ 2.90GHz (6 cores), 16 GB RAM, Ubuntu 18.04.1, bare metal; client and server on the same machine
tradeoffs: Modern header-heavy C++ template design; smaller ecosystem/tooling than gRPC (no multi-language codegen, no official service-mesh integrations).
caveats: The only numbers are a 2019 first-party rest_rpc-vs-brpc doc on the cpp11 branch, which tested the old C++11 version. The link to it from master's README is dead (404), because the doc/ folder is gone from master. The current master README links tests/bench.cpp, which only runs rest_rpc's own echo QPS loop (no gRPC/brpc code, no results). No direct gRPC measurement exists anywhere; 'far exceeds gRPC' is transitive, via brpc's docs/cn/benchmark.md. The benchmark code is partial snippets, and the rest_rpc 'high-efficiency mode' used in the multi-thread runs is undefined. Client timing uses duration_cast<seconds>, so elapsed time has whole-second resolution. The rest_rpc single-thread client uses async_call plus future.wait_for per call.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "rpc" language:c++ --sort stars --limit 30
